speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PROPOSED SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER RELATING TO PRIVATE MEMBERS' HOUR-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Under the terms of Standing Order 15(6) private members' hour on Mondays and Tuesdays is suspended after being reached 40 times. Since this session has been prolonged abnormally, private members now have at their disposal a much smaller proportion of our time than our rules intended. To correct this situation I would move, with unanimous consent, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean):
That beginning on March 1, 1976, and for the remainder of the session, Standing Order 15(6) be suspended.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF EFFECT OF TARIFFS ON EMPLOYMENT IN TEXTILE INDUSTRY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since the economy of the Eastern Townships, in Quebec, depends largely on the textile and clothing industry that provides 32.5 per cent of the jobs in that area, but is now experiencing a serious recession, and in view of the fact that the CSD, Centrale des syndicats democratiques, has just published a report indicating that unemployment in the area could reach 10.6 per cent by the end of April, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That this House now discuss the Canadian tariff policy and its impact on employment and investments in the textile industry, in order to take as soon as possible the necessary steps to support this industry
and ensure that new industrial sectors will be able to absorb the surplus manpower from the textile sector.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PLANS FOR BASE CLOSURES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the concern expressed by the president of the Union of National Defence employees with respect to base closures in the maritime provinces, particularly CFB Shearwater and CFB Greenwood, and the enormously disastrous effect this would have on the Annapolis Valley and the metropolitan area of Dartmouth and Halifax in economic terms, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan):
That the Minister of National Defence not later than Thursday of this week undertake on motions to give to this House, the provincial and municipal authorities involved, the fullest explanation respecting the status of any base closure plans, and to reiterate the firm assurances given by previous Ministers of National Defence and himself that no base closures will take place without the fullest consultation with these officials and this parliament.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED PROVISION FOR RE-OPENING CONTRACT NEGOTIATIONS OF WAGE SETTLEMENT REJECTED BY ANTI-INFLATION BOARD-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that after ten months of negotiations, after assistance from a conciliation commissioner and subsequent consultations with the Anti-Inflation Board, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the National Association of Broadcast Employees and Technicians (NABET) had reached agreement on all issues, including the monetary ones, for a new collective agreement, and in view of the fact that last Wednesday negotiations broke down because the CBC refused to agree to the inclusion of a clause which would permit re-opening of negotiations in the event the AIB reduced the proposed monetary settlement, I move, seconded by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories:
That this House urge the Secretary of State or the Minister of Labour to make clear to the CBC that it is the view of the government that all corporations, whether public or private, as a necessary part of bargaining in good faith during the period in which the anti-inflation program is in effect, should include a clause in all contracts which would lead to the re-opening of negotiations in the event a wage and benefit settlement be rejected by the Anti-Inflation Board.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with a very urgent and important matter, and I am convinced that because of its importance, no hon. member will oppose this motion.
Whereas the Canadian people have very strong feelings on the highly controversial question of capital punishment and that the decision either to abolish or to maintain capital punishment cannot logically be left solely to the Canadian parliamentarians, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House recommend the holding of a referendum on this matter and, in order to avoid an emotional debate, that the time required for holding such a referendum be as short as possible, and that members of the House abstain from campaigning in favour of or against capital punishment so as to really know the views of the Canadian people.

speechtext: As the 1977 estimates show that budgetary spending in fiscal 1976 will be almost $2 billion higher than the forecast in the June 23 budget, would the Prime Minister explain to the House how such massive over-spending could take place in a time of expenditure restraint; and is it now fair for the House to assume that there will be a deficit this year of $5 billion, not $3.2 billion as forecast earlier in the June budget?

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asks for a specific answer to a budgetary question. He should know that the budget is dealt with in a way other than by answering questions.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED INCREASE IN DEFICIT-SOURCE OF FUNDS TO COVER INCREASE-REASON FOR FAILURE TO REVEAL FINANCIAL POSITION
speechtext: A further supplementary question again for the Prime Minister, particularly in view of his reply to my first two questions. Since most groups of working Canadians, whether they be members of a union or a corporation, must now submit their past, current and future financial conditions to the scrutiny of the Anti-Inflation Board, would the Prime Minister indicate why the government is not coming clean with the Canadian people and revealing its own revenue, expenditure and deficit projections to the public, and specifically holding to those projections once they have been revealed?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED INCREASE IN DEFICIT-SOURCE OF FUNDS TO COVER INCREASE-REASON FOR FAILURE TO REVEAL FINANCIAL POSITION

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as one of the older leaders of a party in the House of Commons I have a question for an even older one. I address it to the right hon. Prime Minister. In light of the statement in the white paper on inflation that the government intends to permit the price of oil and gas to rise "toward world levels", and considering that the Premier of Nova Scotia has described such a position as hypocritical because of its lack of consistency with other aspects of the anti-inflation program, I would ask whether the government has given serious reconsideration to including the wellhead price of oil within the framework of the antiinflation guidelines?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I missed the beginning of the question, but I can assure the hon. member that there will be discussions with all the premiers on what the appropriate price of oil should be after the expiration of the present agreement which expires on July 1 next.

OIL-IMPACT PRICE INCREASE ON COST OF LIVING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will direct my supplementary question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Can he inform the House whether the government has now decided to at least not make a commitment to raise the price of oil to world levels, and has his department or any other department of government considered the impact of an increase in the price of oil of say $2 a barrel on the cost of living, and particularly

on the cost of energy in the Maritime provinces where oil is used as the major source of fuel for the production of electricity?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-IMPACT PRICE INCREASE ON COST OF LIVING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member realizes that as a matter of policy the government has been trying to cushion the effects of high international oil prices on the Maritime region. speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN STARTING SEARCH FOR MISSING
subsubtopic: FISHERMEN-POSSIBLE REASSESSMENT OF SEARCH AND RESCUE CAPABILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. It is prompted by a sense of outrage over the loss of two more Canadian fishermen off Canada's east coast, making a total of six so far this year in three separate incidents. My question to the minister is whether he can explain to the House why from the time the fishing boat was reported missing on Sunday to the Halifax Rescue Centre at 7.50 p.m., it took almost 14 hours to get search aircraft into the area which was 500 miles to the east of Halifax.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN STARTING SEARCH FOR MISSING
subsubtopic: FISHERMEN-POSSIBLE REASSESSMENT OF SEARCH AND RESCUE CAPABILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must be referring to the fishing boat, the San Juan. According to my information, it was accompanied by a coastguard vessel. When the National Defence forces were called on, we sent a tracker aircraft and discovered the San Juan which had capsized. We are not yet certain what became of the two persons who were on board. As far as I am aware, the armed forces carried out their duties with great skill and discovered this vessel.

subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN STARTING SEARCH FOR MISSING
subsubtopic: FISHERMEN-POSSIBLE REASSESSMENT OF SEARCH AND RESCUE CAPABILITY
speechtext: May I ask the minister why it took a total of 14 hours to get aircraft into the air from Halifax to the scene which was 500 miles away, and will he undertake to investigate whether or not this costly critical delay could have resulted in the loss of the lives of these two fishermen. Perhaps while he is at it I might ask the minister how many more Canadian fishermen on Canada's east coast have to die before we will have a reassessment of the search and rescue capability of the forces.

subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN STARTING SEARCH FOR MISSING
subsubtopic: FISHERMEN-POSSIBLE REASSESSMENT OF SEARCH AND RESCUE CAPABILITY
speechtext: I will look into those facts, but it certainly does not seem to me that the armed forces would need 14 hours to reach the vessel. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence and arises out of the concern expressed by Mr. Joe Power, president of UNDE and other municipal and provincial authorities in Nova Scotia with respect to widespread rumours, apparently well founded, that consideration is being given by the Minister of National Defence to recommending to his cabinet some time in March that CFB Greenwood be closed and that there be a substantial reduc-

tion in the number of people, both military and civilian, employed at Shearwater. Can the minister indicate to the House whether or not it is a fact that under the base closure program progress in this direction is being considered and, if it is being considered, whether or not, together with that consideration, the assured promises of this minister and his predecessors are being followed with respect to full consultations with the provincial and municipal authorities directly involved.

subtopic: POSSIBLE CLOSURE OF BASES IN NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member used the right terminology when he said there were widespread rumours. As I have said before, we do have the objective of trying to reduce the overhead and the support services in relation to our operating capability, and that study is proceeding. It may mean the reduction of some bases, it may mean an increase in others, it may mean a consolidation of bases. I cannot comment on the individual bases concerned until the study is complete and the recommendations have been made to cabinet.

subtopic: POSSIBLE CLOSURE OF BASES IN NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext: I apologize for my voice, Mr. Speaker. speechtext:
1.	Does it cost twelve dollars to send, by air cargo from New York to Montreal, a letter weighing one ounce in a 10" X 13" envelope and five dollars more to the addressee to clear the said letter at customs and, if so, for what reason?
2.	Are clearance fees provided for in the Act and/or in the Regulations on Customs and Excise and, if not, does the government intend to suggest to Air Canada to end such practice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AIR CARGO RATES AND CHARGES
speechtext:
am informed by the Canadian Transport Commission and the Department of National Revenue as follows: 1. The minimum transportation charge for a single shipment between Montreal and New York is $12. The customs processing minimum charge of $5. is an accessorial charge for the presentation of the shipment for customs clearance.
2.	Clearance fees are not provided for under the Customs Act or regulations, therefore, charges applied by Air Canada do not fall within the purview of Customs and Excise.
3.	Air Canada Air Cargo Tariffs are not specifically approved by the Canadian Transport Commission, but are required to be filed in accordance with the Air Carrier Regulations and are accepted for filing by the Air Transport Committee who have the power to suspend or disallow any tariff, require an air carrier to substitute a tariff or toll satisfactory to the Committee or prescribe another tariff or toll in lieu of any tariff or toll so disallowed. speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
1, 2 and 3. At the end of December 1974, 3,149 applications for pardon were under review. During 1975, 3,210 applications for pardon were received and 1,079 pardons were granted. At the end of December 1975, 5,660 applications were under investigation.
4.	Eight to 12 months.
5.	The long period of time required to process an application for pardon is due to the lengthy and complex investigation done in every case. Furthermore, this investigation involves requesting information from agencies over which we do not exercise administrative control. This situation, impeded by the ever-growing number of requests received and the limited resources with respect to staff within the Clemency and Criminal Records Act Division, has not helped to reduce the period of time required to process an application for pardon. At the present time a study is underway to review the entire process and determine if guidelines could be established which would permit shorter investigation in some circumstances. This study should also establish improved administrative systems for most stages of the investigating process. This study will also help to determine if additional staff is required to meet the ever-growing demand for pardons under the Criminal Records Act. In the meantime, manpower resources have been diverted from other branches of the National Parole Board to reduce the backlog which has accumulated for reasons noted above.

speechtext: The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie).

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I bring to Your Honour's attention that when we were last debating this bill, I believe I called it ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: I am now informed that the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) is correct. He had the floor at the conclusion of the previous debate. The hon. member for Nickel Belt.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I called it ten o'clock at the conclusion of the last time we were debating this bill, I had pointed out that this party considers Bill C-68 a denial and a cutback of a right which this party fought very hard to change for the Canadian people. We fought to have in Canada a Medical Care Act which provided a basic medicare program to those provinces which chose to participate in it. It should be pointed out that the federal government contributes to the cost of medicare to the tune of 50 per cent in any program which a province embarks upon. I pointed out last time that this did not include any special provincial programs for the benefit of their citizens, such as denticare or pharmacare which are paid for 100 per cent by the provinces. The federal government does not put one nickel into those kinds of programs.
Medical Care Act
Bill C-68, which will cut the federal government's contribution to any increase in medicare costs to 13 per cent, places participating provinces on the horns of a dilemma. I previously pointed out that the province of Ontario, for example, was forced to adopt an alternative which the citizens of that province are finding very prejudicial to proper medical care. The Ontario minister of health, without any prior consultation with the communities or staffs involved, is running from hospital to hospital, followed by a coterie of press people, announcing the closing of a hospital here and a hospital there. Rather than cutting back on the federal government's contribution to medicare, this party feels that it should be increased. We should be moving into the field of preventive medicine.
This party has taken a very positive stand with regard to prevention. We have always been in favour of denticare programs because it seemed to us it was much better to identify dental problems early and embark upon remedial work amoung young patients while it was easier and less expensive to do so.
I have stated before that the government stands condemned for its failure to introduce any kind of program with respect to occupational hazards. In particular, the government has a responsibility for occupational health in uranium mines. On the basis of our experience in the uranium mining operation at Elliot Lake, we have pointed out that the government cannot avoid its responsibilities under the Atomic Energy Control Act. The federal government stands condemned for its failure to enforce safety standards under the act. It seems they are prepared to allow these workers to continue mining in very dangerous conditions as a result of which they end up with silicosis or cancer of the lungs. The cost is borne, finally, by the taxpayers of this country, and this is something which should not be necessary.
We have pointed out, too, that among the government's own employees, in the year 1974-75 there were 22,280 accidents which cost our taxpayers $7 million, a figure which does not include the cost of medicare. Where is the government's safety program directed at the welfare of its own workers? We feel a great deal could be done to cut costs by developing an industrial safety program in this area. Where are the priorities in this country? We are prepared to spend over a billion dollars for the Olympics. There is no stopping of the taps when it comes to that event; we let the expenditure go up and up. We saw only the other day that a parking lot for cars is to cost $60 million instead of $30 million. Bread and circuses: they will be the downfall of the government across the way. As I say, we are prepared to spend over a billion dollars for a two-week performance of muscle-building by a very select group of athletes, while we do not appear to be concerned about embarking upon a program of preventive medical care in this country.
We in this party have urged greater use of paramedics as a means of improving health standards generally. We have called attention to the fact that out-patient facilities are sadly lacking. Far from cutting back expenditure in this area, this is one direction in which we should be increasing it. The government does not need to concern itself about disciplining the provinces, bearing in mind the provinces themselves have to contribute 50 per cent of the cost of the

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
medicare program. In addition, they must pay 100 per cent of the cost of any special programs upon which they may choose to embark.
The party to which I belong has urged the minister responsible to withdraw this bill. We are making this suggestion again today in very positive terms. The government ought to withdraw the bill and seek ways in which to implement a program of preventive medicine, as well as means by which reasonable steps could be taken to economize, if hon. members opposite so desire. Pushing the bill through the House now can only result in actions by the provinces which will be deleterious to the health of their people; it will force them to set priorities which involve the saving of money in very narrow areas.
One would assume the government would agree that the idea of bringing together the ministers of health was a good one. After all, the party opposite has always talked about participatory democracy. What happened to that notion? If he has the health of the people in mind, it is surely not beyond the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to call together his provincial colleagues and talk this matter out with them once more. We know already how it is affecting the people of Ontario, for example. The minister of health of that province does not consult with the municipalities or with the communities concerned. He does not consult with the staff of the hospitals who are affected by his decisions. For dramatic effect, he drives around in a big limousine announcing he is closing this hospital or that hospital. He zaps them!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: What?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
I said "zap". By doing so, he creates a problem for the community concerned. That is not a reasonable way of determining priorities, it seems to me. I suppose it is the Liberal way of doing things.
I would direct attention, now, to a field with which we have concerned ourselves very little, the field of mental health. A reasonable way to approach this problem, it seems to me, would be by making treatment programs available to school boards to enable early identification of young people who might be encountering emotional problems so that ways could be found of helping such persons adjust to the situation. Instead of providing adequate facilities and personnel to make this possible, it seems we are prepared to let this situation boil over, and when a problem is created for society we shall simply lock these people up and throw away the key while we run around demanding what we call law and order. To my way of thinking we could spend, with advantage, a lot more money on the treatment and care of the mentally afflicted. Again, this is a subject which might well be discussed at a meeting of the health ministers.
Again I call upon the government to withdraw this bill and reconsider the whole question at a meeting with the provincial ministers, in an effort to arrive at a solution of the problem in a way which would be much more appealing and satisfactory to the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a responsibility for a member to address himself to an important piece of legislation. We have a great deal of legislation before us. I sometimes think we have become

something of a legislative treadmill. We never seem to catch up with our order paper or get down to what we have planned to do. For instance, I think that after ten years it is time we disposed of the national anthem bill one way or the other.
In these times it is important to make a major effort to produce legislation of vital content. In the days of Mackenzie King and R. B. Bennett there used to be two parliamentary sessions a year. Under the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) we have two years per session, so it is very confusing as to what is priority legislation. But if I were a man capable of righteous indignation, I would be indignant about this particular bill. I do not make any pretence to being a righteous man, nor am I often indignant, but I believe this bill is the most serious, hurtful and dangerous piece of legislation that I have seen in all the years I have been here-which is now nearly a score. It is dangerous, hurtful and iniquitous because it is doing just the opposite to what the representatives of the people in this people's institution should be doing.
If there is any maxim that should govern us, which should direct those who govern the state, it is clearly that those in society who most need help should be helped the most. Today we find ourselves in the midst of an austerity program. We are in an anti-inflation mood. And who are the chief targets of the operation? The elderly people.
Not long ago, Mr. Speaker, we knocked off the unemployment roll the poor old guys who had worked for years and years. When they reached 65 years of age they were told, "It's too bad, but you are out of luck". We are now doing this with the sick. I agree with what the former speaker said. A lot of nonsense comes out of the NDP corner, and I have been listening to it for many years; but they are not always wrong. I am appalled to read about hospitals being closed. The only way that policy can be justified in a civilized society would be if we had reached the stage where the hospitals had empty beds. Yet we all know that thousands and thousands of Canadians want hospital care and are not able to get it. People all over this country have been told, "Yes, we might get you in in 9 months, 10, or perhaps 15. But unless it is a terrible emergency, unless you have a 50 per cent chance of dying tomorrow, you won't get in".
Despite all the slick optimism of a publication called "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians", we all know that today we are not providing adequate health services for the Canadian people. To bring in a piece of legislation that is clearly designed to diminish the effectiveness and the range of services now being offered is-and I choose my words carefully-criminal injustice. It is an outrage to the sick people of this country, to the people who most need compassion, who most need care and who most need to be in the thoughts of all of us here today.
I thought my colleague from Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) came out with a very fine truism. He expressed it in a very articulate way in this debate a few days ago when he said that health is not a privilege that should be tied to the bank account of the state. I am not a stubborn man, but no one can convince me that there is any justice, rationale or wisdom in making a move to strengthen the economy by
February 24, 1976

hitting at the sick, the infirm, the aged and the ill in our society. It is repugnant, and should be repugnant to any man or woman of compassion as he or she views the needs of the Canadian people.
My former leader, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), has taken part in this debate; I think it was the last speech he made on a piece of legislation in this chamber. It was very appropriate that he did enter the debate and bring to bear his great wisdom, broad experience and deep compassion. One of the great privilieges in my public life has been the opportunity of serving under the hon. member for Halifax. We in this country sometimes foolishly talk about the ideology of right and left, which actually has no bearing upon Canadian public life at all but is an imported European term. In the connection, the values and the problems relating to the people of Canada the hon. gentleman was right in the moral sense. He was just, he was compassionate and concerned. I am immensely proud of what he said the other day. During the years that he has been here as our leader he has never forsaken the same maxim I repeated at the beginning of my remarks-that a government must care for those who most need care.
I note, too, that another member who engaged in the debate was a former premier of Saskatchewan, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). He is a socialist; that is, if the NDP are still socialists. They do not talk much about that. He, too, has been a great humanitarian. He is a man who knows and cares about the problems of the poor, the dispossessed, the suffering, the infirm. I think the country should know that the two former premiers in this House spoke eloquently and with feeling on this particular measure. I endorse their views.
The hon. member who has just spoken was quite right in suggesting that this most reprehensible piece of legislation should be put in cold storage, or perhaps frozen forever, and that we should have consultation with the provinces in regard to this subject. The two major iniquities in this bill are on the side of compassion and care for people and, as my former leader said, care for confederation. You cannot build a strong country by knocking around the health services. You cannot build a healthy tomorrow by closing hospitals and forcing upon the provinces a diminution in medical care grants. You cannot build a healthy Canada if the word of the federal government given to the provinces is not respected or honoured.
I was in this House when medicare was launched. I remember very well the four-point formula that was put forward and what the spokesmen for the provinces said at that time. Many of them were reluctant to accept medicare. Some were upset, others disturbed. But in the end they had to accept, and did accept-and I believe they were right in accepting this for their people in the long run-the four-point program. Now, having gone through all that exercise, they hear that, unilaterally, the central government has changed the rules and has put upon each province a burden impossible to bear, while hurting the very people who can least stand an assault from a narrow-minded government in a belated binge of penny-pinching.
What is confederation but a continuing relationship of faith and understanding between constituent parties?
Medical Care Act
Every province entered under special arrangements and negotiations. Some of them were under the British North America Act and some were put there subsequently; but the whole basis of this continuing experiment was that a word was given as valid. An agreement once entered upon is changed by discussions, by negotiation and not by a fiat of the office of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. That is not the way to keep the country going. Although we love our country and are filled with hopes for its future, let us not think there is something inevitable or that this country can automatically sustain the fabric of confederation, or that it is not capable of being torn apart. It is frail fabric, confederation. It always has been and it has required wisdom, moderation, consideration and concern to hold the country together.
The most important element in holding this country together is, was, and has to be, the national government, the national institutions-the very things which are common to all Canadians. If you have bad faith at the centre of the institutions of the nation, and 4f you have unilateral declarations and sudden fiats from one of the partners of confederation, then not only the health of the people but the health of our society, of our political institutions, of our parliamentary democracy, of politics itself and of confederation are assaulted; and this country cannot stand that kind of assault.
I should think that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) would prove himself a big man if he could stand up some day-perhaps today-and say, "All of us are prone to error. I and my colleagues have made a mistake. We have reflected upon it, and we are going to withdraw the bill." He would find that in this opposition group, although we are much invigorated-that is why we have such fighting, young people speaking now-we are still understanding and agreeable. We will help him withdraw, we will turn over a new page, we will redirect him to the problems so that he may come out with something sensible. Perhaps the minister could then come forth with some careful consideration. He could talk to the ministers from all the provinces and assess with them the needs of the nation. He should remember that you do not break your word and keep the country strong. You do not harass, distress and beset the suffering and build a just society, a new society or a good society.
This is an outrageous piece of legislation. It is built upon shortsightedness, a regrettable tendency toward what I am afraid is showmanship, and a break in the economy in the very area that cannot be sustained. It is bad faith, and it is tearing at the vitals of confederation.
I think the minister has tried hard in his portfolio. He has sometimes been too autocratic both inside the House and outside. I do not think he is a foolish man. I think he wants to do a decent job. But he has been far too prone to foolish optimism. The book to which I referred, "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians", is slick, nonsensical, stupid optimism of the worst kind. The suggestion that in this country we have so many doctors we do not need any more, and we are not going to let anyone else come in, is nonsensical.
There are thousands of Canadians who today are living miles and miles from medical services; old people fearful that in the middle of winter, and perhaps in the middle of

the night, they may want the services of a doctor. My good friend, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald)-from that prime province of the whole Dominion, Prince Edward Island-knows that there are people in that category, old people living in fear. Yet we read and hear that we have so many doctors we do not need any more. That, too, is an outrage.
It is also an outrage that as the years have gone by we have not provided for the training of more qualified medical people in this country. If we ever reach the stage-and we are a long way from it-where we have an abundance of doctors, there are, God knows, many parts of the world which could benefit from their services. Our medical schools should be enlarged and there should be more of them. We should be turning out more medical people. I have never been very attracted to the suggestion of these closed societies among certain professionals because they are, like all of us-or should be-devoted to the service of their fellow citizens rather than building closed shops.
I add my voice to those who condemn this bill, and that is a heavy word that I do not often use. I condemn it because it is wrong it terms of compassion, and I condemn it because it is dangerous to the unfolding and developing of confederation. There is no way that bad faith can be the foundation of good legislation. There is no way that aiming at the weaker elements of society, the people in need, can become just. This measure is wrong and improperly inspired, if I may use that word. It is wrong in detail, it is wrong in principle, and it is hurtful to confederation.
I make this appeal on behalf of the thousands of Canadians who need friends. It is tough enough to be sick, but it is harder when you read every day that it is going to be more and more difficult to get the kind of attention that might bring you through a debilitating illness back to that great glory of life, the feeling of good health. I say, also, that at a time when tensions within our country are very severe and the centrifugal forces are far too strong, it ill behooves the federal government to be acting in such a way toward the provinces in an area so sensitive to human need and so sensitive to the principle of confederation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on Bill C-68 I think it appropriate that, as a layman in these matters, I should try to express the feelings of some of the very able and distinguished members of the medical profession in my own constituency of Medicine Hat and perhaps of their counterparts throughout the province of Alberta. This is what I propose to do in my contribution to this important debate.
First of all, let us go back to Monday, June 23, 1975, when the then minister of finance presented the budget speech in the House of Commons. The minister stated that in light of the existing inflationary environment, his government was committed to restraining public expenditure. One of the major expenditure restraint programs announced in that budget was related to the two main statutory programs in the health field, namely, hospital and medical care insurance. The minister defended his government's decision to introduce controls in respect of these programs by stating that the annual increase in their cost had, on average, run well ahead of the growth of the national

income and had increased 19.8 per cent over the previous year. The measures announced by the minister to control the increasing cost of health care have created a great deal of concern among the medical profession.
I propose to examine the measures designed to limit federal contributions to the provinces under the Medical Care Act and some of the potential implications of this program. In order to understand the government's program to limit federal contributions to the provinces under the Medical Care Act, it is necessary to have an understanding of the cost-sharing formula. The formula which is contained in the Medical Care Act basically calls for the government to contribute to each province half the average per capita cost of all insured services for all participating provinces, multiplied by the number of insured persons within the province. Under this formula, a major proportion of the total provincial medical care cost is provided by the federal government to those provinces in which the per capita cost of medical care is lower than the national average. The following quotation is taken directly from the minister's budget speech of last June:
A second measure aimed at more effective cost control involves the establishment of a ceiling on the yearly rise in the contributions the federal government makes to the provinces under the Medical Care Act. Since provincial administrations will need some time to adjust their planning, this ceiling will be made effective for 1976, and subsequent years. More specifically a ceiling will be placed on the per capita rate of growth of federal contributions to provinces. This ceiling will be 13 per cent in 1976-77, 10 V2 per cent in 1977-78, and 8V2 per cent in 1978-79, and subsequent years. The per capita approach means that varying rates of population growth between provinces, or from year to year will be automatically taken into account in total contributions to provinces.
The Medical Care Act operates under a fiscal year ending March 31. This means that the year April 1, 1975, to March 31, 1976, will be the base year upon which the ceiling for the federal contribution will be calculated. For example, if the average rate of per capita cost for medical care services is $100 in the 1975-76 fiscal year, the maximum average rate per capita cost upon which the federal government would compute payment to each province for 1976-77 would be $113.
There are two fundamental problems with the proposed federal controls as outlined in the budget speech of the minister. The proposed ceilings amount to price controls on physicians' services. No other sector of the economy had been subjected to wage or price controls at that time. Again referring to last June 23, 1975, the second major shortcoming is that the proposed price ceilings must make allowance for several variables which directly affect real physician income such as increases in utilization, increased number of physicians, overhead and inflation. Despite the lack of stability in these variables, the proposed ceilings appear to be inflexible.
Before examining the implications of the ceilings on federal contributions to Alberta, it is worth while to determine whether in fact control is justified. In his budget speech, the minister stated that the previous year federal contributions to the provinces in respect of the hospital and medical care insurance programs had to be increased 19.8 per cent over the year before. The average per capita medical care cost for the ten major provinces rose only 5.9 per cent from the fiscal year ended March 31, 1973, to the fiscal year ended March 31, 1974.
February 24, 1976

It can be shown that the annual increase in average per capita medicare costs for Canada from 1971 to 1974 averaged 6.9 per cent. From 1971 to 1974 the average annual increase in per capita GNP at market prices was 12.8 per cent. Furthermore, from June, 1971, to June, 1974, the Canadian consumer price index rose an average of 7.9 per cent annually, while average weekly wages and salaries rose 8.5 per cent annually. The increases in per capita medicare costs in Alberta have been substantially below those of Canada as a whole. From 1970 to 1974, the annual rate of increase in per capita medicare costs in Alberta averaged only 3.8 per cent. In the same period of time, per capita gross domestic product in Alberta rose 13.6 per cent annually. Further, from June, 1970, to June, 1974, the consumer price index for Edmonton and Calgary averaged an annual increase of 5.7 per cent, while average weekly wages and salaries in Alberta averaged an increase of 8.6 per cent annually.
I want to point out that the physicians of Alberta have demonstrated a great deal of responsibility in controlling increases in the cost of medicare. For example, in 1971 the per capita cost of medical care in Alberta was almost identical to the national average. By 1974, Alberta's per capita cost of medicare services was 12.6 per cent less than the national average. This has resulted in the federal government assuming a larger proportion of the total Alberta medicare costs. From 1971 to 1974, the percentage of total costs for insured services in Alberta, paid for by the federal government, increased from 48.6 per cent to 56.3 per cent because Alberta is operating at a lower cost.
Further, federal contributions, plus premiums, are almost sufficient to pay for the total cost of basic medical services. It is only when the costs of chiropractic, optomet-ric, podiatric, oral surgery and osteopathic services, as well as Alberta health care administrative costs are added, that the province of Alberta must contribute. The province of Alberta contributed $3.9 million in 1971, $8.7 million in 1972, $10 million in 1973, and $17.5 million in 1974.
Mr. Speaker, the foregoing suggests that per capita medicare costs in Canada, and especially in Alberta, have not been increasing at an unreasonable rate. Furthermore, the government of Alberta has not been required to subsidize the cost of medicare to any great extent. No one denies that total health care costs are increasing rapidly, but the responsibility for these large increases does not lie with medicare payments.
Now I should like to make some comments on the increases in these medicare payments. Legislation to impose the ceiling on federal contributions as outlined in the budget speech was drafted and received first reading in the House last July 8. Bill C-68 also contains the clause which excludes new insured services from the ceiling on federal cost-sharing. A new insured service is defined as- a health service prescribed after June 23,1975, by the minister pursuant to subsection 4(3) that was furnished pursuant to a medical care insurance plan of the province at a time during the first twelve months in which that health service was deemed by subsection 4(3) to be, in respect of that province, a service rendered by a medical practitioner that is medically required.
To examine the impact of Bill C-68 as it is currently written, we shall assume for the time being that the gov-
Medical Care Act
eminent of Alberta will not allow medicare payments to Alberta physicians to increase at a rate higher than the ceilings proposed by the federal government. I think this is a fair assumption. This would then amount to a global budgeting situation, with substantial declines in real physician income. There are several factors beyond the control of physicians which will reduce increases in average net physician income to a level far below that of the proposed ceilings. A real increase in total medicare payments to physicians should theoretically be an increase in income for providing the same number of equal medical services. Allowance must be made to pay for providing more medical services from the increase in total medicare payments as governed by the ceilings in Bill C-68. The demand for more medical services is a function of increased population and increased utilization. Another major factor in reducing average net physician income will be an increasing number of physicians sharing a limited pool of funds. Finally, rising costs of overhead will have to be paid for out of the increases as governed by Bill C-68.
To examine the combined impact of these factors upon average net physician income, taking into account the increases as proposed by Bill C-68, we shall first estimate what the future increases in the variables might be. We shall then utilize a hypothetical case to determine the proportion of the increases that the average Alberta physician would receive as increased net income. As mentioned previously, the demand for more medical services is a function of increased population and increased utilization. However, the federal government has indicated that the federal contribution to the provinces will be calculated on a per capita basis, which means that increased cost due to increasing population will not have to be accounted for within the ceilings proposed in Bill C-68.
However, no allowance has been made for increased utilization of medical services. Two major reasons for increasing utilization are that with reduced birth rates and longer life expectancy, there is a shift in the age distribution of the population toward the older segments who traditionally require more medical services. Since 1971, utilization in Alberta-measured by the total number of medical services per 1,000 persons-has increased at an average annual rate of about 2 per cent. Increases in average gross medicare payments to physicians will be considerably lower than the ceilings proposed under Bill C-68 because of increasing numbers of physicians sharing the pie. From 1964 to 1974, the number of Alberta physicians registered with the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta averaged an annual increase of 5.1 per cent. From 1971 to 1974, registration with the college averaged a yearly increase of 3.7 per cent. In the same period of time, the number of physicians receiving payments from the AHCIC has increased an average of 4.3 per cent annually. It therefore seems reasonable to project that the average annual rate of increase in the number of physicians in Alberta will be approximately 4 per cent.
The Department of National Health and Welfare publication "Earnings of Physicians in Canada" reported that overhead consumed 37.4 per cent of gross professional earnings of Alberta physicians in 1972. This overhead percentage was equivalent to $16,620 of the average gross AHCIC payments to physicians in 1972. From 1972 to 1974, average gross AHCIC payments to physicians increased

only 9 per cent, while overhead costs have risen substantially in the light of inflation. The major components of increasing total overhead included increasing cost of rent, medical supplies and the unprecedented increases in salaries of allied health personnel. For example, in 1975 registered nurses received effective salary increases of about 33 per cent, certified nursing aides received a 48 per cent increase, laboratory and X-ray technologists received average increases of 35 per cent, and clerical staff in hospitals received average increases of approximately 40 per cent.
In the light of inadequate increases in average gross AHCIC payments and rapidly increasing overhead costs since 1972, it is estimated that for the average Alberta physician overhead will consume 45 per cent of professional earnings in 1975. This would represent an average 12.5 per cent annual increase in actual overhead dollars from 1972 to 1975. For the purpose of illustration, it has been conservatively estimated that overhead dollars will increase 10 per cent annually from 1976 onward.
Let us assume that the government of Alberta will not increase the proportion of total medicare costs paid for from the coffers of the province. We shall also assume that the government of Alberta is well aware that increased utilization will result in an increase in the number of medical services of approximately 2 per cent annually. It follows that the largest increase to physicians that the Alberta government would be willing to negotiate would be the federal ceiling, less 2 per cent. In other words, the maximum increase for 1976-77 would be 11 per cent, 8.5 per cent for 1977-78, and 6.5 per cent for 1978-79 and subsequent years.
To illustrate the impact of these effective ceilings on net physician income, let us assume that total payments to 2,400 Alberta physicians for insured medical care services were $120 million in the 1975-76 base year. With the previously determined estimates for increasing numbers of physicians and increasing overhead, average net physician income will increase only 4.1 per cent in 1976-77 and will actually begin to decline in 1977-78 and subsequent years. By the 1977-78 fiscal year the moneys required to compensate for increased overhead and increasing numbers of physicians will exceed the total dollar increase in medicare payments. This, of course is the reason for declining net income from 1977-78 onward.
This decline in average net physician income will be further exacerbated by general inflation in the economy which will reduce real net physician income. The Economic Council of Canada, in its eleventh annual review, showed that the incidence of inflation is about the same for all families, regardless of their income level. From December, 1972, to December, 1974, the consumer price index for Edmonton and Calgary rose 21.3 per cent. The latest Statistics Canada figures show that the Canadian CPI rose 11.1 per cent from July, 1974, to July, 1975. If it is conservatively estimated that the consumer price index will increase 9 per cent annually to 1980, it can be calculated that average net physician income, expressed 1975-76 constant dollars, will decline 34.5 per cent by the 1979-80 fiscal year.

It can be shown that Bill C-68 does not adequately take into account such factors as increased population, utilization, number of physicians, overhead and inflation. If this bill is legislated, average net income in Alberta will decline substantially. This is obviously unacceptable to Alberta physicians as it can be illustrated that since the advent of medicare in Alberta the average real net income of the average physician has decreased almost 40 per cent. Alberta physicians require substantial increases in average gross income merely to regain the real net income received several years ago. I have demonstrated that there is no justification for the federal government imposing controls upon increases in medicare payments when the average annual rate of increase in per capita costs for Alberta has averaged only 3.8 per cent since 1970. A consequence of higher standards of medical care can be increased costs. If unreasonable cost controls are introduced, it is possible that health care standards could be adversely affected. Further, the physicians of Alberta may have no alternative but to look more to the patient in order to maintain income.
I think it is obvious that I cannot agree with the intent of this bill, and I certainly share the feelings which my colleague from Prince Edward Island expressed in his remarks just before mine. Surely we should at least set this bill aside until the new control and restraint policy which we are now endeavouring to put into effect has had a chance to operate.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be delighted to hear the parliamentary secretary when I have finished. My speech is nearing its conclusion. I shall have something to say about the parliamentary secretary too. The Minister of National Health and Welfare thinks he looks big and brave because he saved Canadians from an American football intrusion. But he has done little to correct Canadian environmental difficulties, and this makes him look small.
Let me discuss other issues which the minister raised. What has the minister done to correct drug abuse in Canada? I include cigarettes among drugs, as well as heroin, marijuana and other drugs? I will tell you: he has done little, to his shame. The minister whom we thought was progressive and compassionate is hiding behind a jurisdictional wall, saying, "Probably all we can do is introduce some kind of educational program." Is that how we are to correct this difficulty? If little or nothing is done to correct drug abuse, it will be to the minister's everlasting shame and discredit.
What has the minister done with regard to child abuse? Not long ago the minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs so ably chaired by the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson). Both ministers made wide-ranging speeches voicing their concern over child abuse. Both said it was necessary to correct child abuse. Last week the committee heard the testimony of two most competent witnesses on child abuse. One was Bryon Gero and the other was Professor Cyril Greenland of the Ontario Association of Professional Social Workers. They told the committee many of the problems concerning child abuse. Bryon Gero said that we need a commonly understood definition of child abuse, a central registry, provisions for mandatory reporting of child abuse and, more importantly, preventive programs. He told the committee what the Minister of National Health and Welfare ought to do if we are to correct child abuse. He said that we need demographic information concerning housing and social service needs-an excellent point.
He said that we need programs which will strengthen family life and improve social services and education- another excellent point. He said, further, that we need

detection programs involving schools, police, social workers, hospitals and doctors. We need to solve premarital problems, and need assessment services which will take into account family relationships. We need marriage and group counselling services and services to examine behavioural problems. He seems to say that we need, immediately, a guaranteed income plan and better day-care programs,
I hope that the parliamentary secretary, who is a member of the committee, will tell the minister what Bryon Gero told the committee and convey to the House how necessary it is to introduce the guaranteed annual income and more day-care centres if we are to eliminate child abuse.
We then had Professor Greenland, who indicated a research experience arising out of a program in which he studied 100 persons who were not guilty of violent crimes by reason of insanity, another 100 persons guilty and in penitentiaries for violent crimes, another 96 persons who were dangerous sexual offenders, and another 65 persons who committed murder followed by suicide. The common denominator that he found with regard to the study was that there was a severe deprivation in childhood for all these people in some of the basic cares, needs and protections that they required. He pointed out that there was a high degree of the passing on of tendencies with regard to these people who suffered severe deprivation in their childhood. He also pointed out that a great number of the cases occurred as a result of alcohol and drug abuse. I would underline that fact to the parliamentary secretary.
He also pointed out that even though there had been adequate warning in 50 per cent of the cases-in other words, from the mother or the person seeking help-there was a failure to deal with the person seeking help. He said there has not been a serious epidemic of child abuse, but if conditions prevail there is a possibility that there will be. He pointed out how much research and identification is needed, with regard to this problem, and the necessity of programs to deal with these people.
In the minds of many people throughout this country, child abuse is one area where the Minister of National Health and Welfare could make a great contribution toward lessening the impact of the problem. What does he do? I fear I know what he is going to do. He is going to say that this is within provincial jurisdiction, and the government will try their best to give a few pennies to research. Instead of stimulating the provinces to take action and supplying moneys to develop research and programs so that we can have prevention, the minister does little or nothing. This is what he has done so far.
I want to deal with what some of the Liberal members have said in their speeches, especially the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Rail-ton). I am sorry he is not here this afternoon. He replaces another Liberal member. I am sure all who knew Don Tolmie would say that without doubt he was a concerned and compassionate person. When I hear the remarks of the parliamentary secretary they send shivers down my spine. He said that the main unserviced areas in medical care are the frontiers. I take strong exception to that statement.
If the parliamentary secretary had heard what the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) said
February 24, 1976

with regard to the problems in East Richmond, he would realize how necessary it is to expand medical and hospital services in the maritimes. I am sure that members from Newfoundland, Quebec, the prairie provinces, the north, and British Columbia can repeat the problems that they have with regard to the shortage of medical care. When the parliamentary secretary talks about a shortage on the frontiers, he is right. However, the frontiers are not only in the outlying areas; they are in the inlying areas in the main cities.
The hon. member for Spadina, who has a constituency fairly adjacent to mine, and the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Roberts), can tell you of the number of people who have related to us their problems with regard to medical and hospital care. There is not a shadow of doubt with regard to the shortage of medical hospital services in the city of Toronto. I am sure the same thing applies to other main cities across the province.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs compared Canadian medical services to United States medical services. He said that U.S. medical services are as good, if not better, than Canadian services. Any person who has experienced U.S. medical care services realizes that it is not difficult to beat or to better them. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) set forth the problem of a civil servant who went to Florida at Christmas with his wife and children. His child became ill and he took the child to the hospital. The greeting he received at the hospital was that if he placed $1,500 to the deposit of that hospital, they would take care of the child. A person whom I know lives in Florida a few months of the year. I asked why he did not stay there permanently. He said he could not afford to become ill in Florida; he has to come back to Canada to protect himself and his family. It is passing strange that Senator Ted Kennedy would come to Canada, study our program, praise it and want to implement it as part of the Democratic party's campaign in the next election, yet the parliamentary secretary wants us to take the American experience and the American service.
I wish to deal for a few minutes with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Kaplan). He stated that 6.9 per cent of our gross national product goes to medicare, compared to 7.7 per cent in the United States. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, as a very reasonable and understanding person, what relationship our gross national product should have to medical services. None whatsoever. The test should be that every Canadian is entitled to full and adequate medical and hospital care. That is the test we should apply to education, pensions, housing and unemployment. Every person in Canada is entitled to employment, to decent housing, to decent medical services and to a decent pension. That should be the test. There should not be a relationship to the gross national product. I can see the parliamentary secretary shaking his head and asking, "Where are we going to get the money?" What is necessary is that we arrange our priorities to look after the basic needs of the people.
I was rather proud to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last night on television when he dealt with the delegation from the chambers of commerce and read a few excerpts from their brief which said the government
Medical Care Act
should cut its spending in this area and that area. Nowhere in the brief was there any mention of cuts in the area of corporate welfare. The government, they argued, should cut its spending in housing and on social services but should not consider for one moment cutting down the billions the corporations received.
It would be fair to ask what the NDP would do with regard to medicare. Look at our record. We stand tall and proud when we think of the medical services we have provided in Canada. Let me name them. In 1947, the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) introduced hospitalization insurance in Saskatchewan. In 1962 he introduced the medicare program in Saskatchewan. The NDP has introduced medicare programs in Manitoba and in British Columbia, of which we are justly proud. We have added dental and pharmacare and we have developed community clinics and out-patient facilities which the people of those provinces appreciate and wish to protect.
Look at the Tory record. I give them credit for closing the loophole in 1958 in the Liberal legislation which stated that hospitalization programs would be constituted on a national scale when a majority of the provinces, representing a majority of the population, consented. I give the Tories credit for closing that loophole. I give them credit, too, for establishing a royal commission under the able leadership of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall. That commission produced one of the best reports on health care we have ever seen. Also, I must, reluctantly, give credit to the Liberal government under the late Lester Pearson in 1968 for finally introducing medicare insurance across the country. But when one comes to think of it, Mackenzie King said in 1919 that part of the Liberal program would be to institute hospital medical care. But it took from 1919 to 1968 to put that program into operation.
I notice that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) is here with us. It would be fair for me to say that he was the minister responsible for bringing forward that legislation, and for doing so he deserves the gratitude of all Canadians.
