speechtext:
Madam Speaker, for one who has been in the House of Commons a number of years this is rather a sad occasion-I am taking my handkerchief out already. To see a once vigorous and creative government coasting to a conclusion in this way, even for members of the opposition brings a certain sense of sadness. I have been involved in all the debates giving rise to the excellent medicare program that we now have in Canada. The spirit of rising expectations moved us forward in 1958 when the then Conservative government-in this regard I appreciate the complimentary words of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert)-brought in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This was a great breakthrough in medical care for Canadians on a universal basis.
I think everyone will admit that it is the cost of hospitalization that breaks the financial back of families. Anyone who has had chronic illness in their family knows that hospital bills can leap forward to $25,000, $50,000, even to $75,000; and no family, regardless of its means, can stand financial burdens of that kind. We then came to 1968 when, based on the excellent report of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, the Medical Care Act was passed by the Pearson government.
Now we seem to be marching backwards. When the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) was leader of the opposition, he put the situation in very nice perspective, using the proper words, when he said that the government was busy drowning its own brainchildren. This is yet another example. The official opposition has just been reinvigorated by the election of a new, young and energetic leader, and I am hoping that this dramatic transformation in the political affairs of the nation will reverse the trend in public affairs that has become all too obvious in recent years.
Just to quote the spirit that prevails in government ranks as expressed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) as recently as 1974 when he presented his white paper on medicare in Canada, as recorded at page 5 of the report he said:
Good health is the bedrock on which social progress is built. A nation of healthy people can do those things that make life worth while, as the level of health increases so does the potential for happiness.
Obviously, Bill C-68 is, as hon. members who have spoken have described it, a thoroughly bad bill and will certainly do nothing to increase the potential for happiness of the Canadian people. The Secretary of State for Exter-

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
nal Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), who is in the House today, made many significant and optimistic statements in respect of health care in Canada some years ago when we were waiting for contemplated action on the Hall report. He said:
Health is not a privilege tied to the state of one's bank account, but rather a basic right which should be open to all.
I trust that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is busy in conversation, has not forgotten those words. Hopefully, he will take part in this debate to reinforce the spirit of enthusiasm and creativity regarding health services expressed in those remarks which he made some ten years ago.
We have all been proud of the fact that Canada has a fine and outstanding medicare program. Indeed, when Canadians tended to become slightly hyperbolic we used to say it was the finest medicare program in the world. We are now running into problems of higher and rising costs. This was to be expected, as outlined when we took part in the debate back in 1968. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) predicted this would be the case unless priorities were stressed, unless the preventive aspect of health care were stressed and unless the second stage, as it was described by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), were adopted. He said the passing of the hospital diagnostic act and the approval of the medicare act was only the beginning, and that these would do nothing to deal with the real problems of medicare and health in the nation other than to provide an adequate basis of financial support. The second and inevitable stage, with which we have really never come to grips, was the organization of a program of education and prevention that would provide the best possible medical services at the least possible cost.
This government, which has lost its zeal for the just society, has lost its momentum and is now coasting downhill to an inevitable conclusion. It has lost its vision and has come up with a simplistic solution. It has decided that putting an arbitrary ceiling on federal contributions will solve all the problems of the medicare program. This is as simplistic as the government's approach to inflation which was once described as the major attack of the government in wrestling inflation to the ground. The bill is very brief, consisting only of three pages. Its very brevity indicates that a simplistic solution has been applied to what is an extremely complex problem. To put the matter in proper perspective, perhaps we should look back on how we came to have the outstanding health care program that is Canada's resulting from action in the 1950s and 1960s.
At the time the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act was passed in 1958 there was a great and growing need for this basic hospital care program. There was agitation for a follow up with some sort of medicare financial protection program. Based on the hospital insurance act, some provinces seized the initiative and moved into this further area of development. Saskatchewan, with a great and noisy debate, led the way. Manitoba chose the road of voluntary health insurance, as did Ontario.
I remember, at the time the Government of Canada was insisting that every province conform to the compulsory program, it was proposing there was considerable resistance on the part of the province of Manitoba because it had
[Mr. Dinsdale.j
a very successful and broad coverage under a voluntary program operated by the physicians of Manitoba. At the federal government's insistence, Manitoba was forcefully brought into line with the federal compulsory program. This has been dealt with by several speakers as the beginning of the federal invasion into the area of provincial prerogatives in respect of health and welfare. This led to the statement of the then minister of finance in the province of Ontario, the Hon. Charles MacNaughton, who said, "We have started down the slippery slope of fiscal irresponsibility, with the result that we are now faced with a further arbitrary and almost bewildering invasion of the prerogatives of provincial jurisdiction."
No wonder provincial governments of all stripes, and without exception, reacted with indignation and bewilderment when the program was first announced in the budget last June. Let me quote the immediate response of the minister of health and social development from my own province of Manitoba. He said this in a telegram of June 25, 1975:
Your government's decision to proceed with major changes on a unilateral basis is a serious disappointment to our province and, I assume, to most others ... Not only does the decision represent an apparent breach of our earlier understanding ... (in January)
Let me interpolate by saying the government is still confused in this time of wrestling with inflation. According to the statement of the minister of health for Manitoba, it reversed itself from decisions and agreements that had been reached at the earlier conference in January. Of course, this is not the only reversal of the government. It reversed itself 180 degrees on prices and incomes policy without any warning other than the resignation of the then minister of finance. His resignation must have been based on his disagreement with this zig-zagging approach of the Government of Canada. Let me resume the quotation as follows:
Not only does the decision represent an apparent breach of our earlier understanding (in January) but also, and more importantly, it suggests that your government has every intention of implementing legislative changes which will cause the primary financial reponsibility for the future reform of health care and for the maintenance of existing service standards to be borne by the provincial governments and their taxpayers ... It is obvious that such a decision would represent a significant threat to our national health standards ... standards based on a system which the federal government itself initiated.
That was on June 25 last year, from the province of Manitoba. That was followed by the statement of the province of Ontario, at the Victoria conference which was mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Broadview.
It was said they have very much to lose by this change in federal government policy because a heavy financial burden will fall upon them. The hon. member for Broadview attempted to severely castigate the province of Ontario in its attempt to deal with the financial problems that are already beginning to be felt. The minister of health for Manitoba, speaking at the Victoria conference that had been convened at the request of the government of Ontario, said:
I think they (provincial premiers) will want to know what justification the federal government has for apparently choosing to make these essential programs one of the main targets of its campaign against
February 24, 1976

inflation-even though it is obvious that the benefits these programs provide in terms of real income protection are among the most important safeguards we have against inflation for the low and middle income people in this country-and especially for the pensioners, the people who probably have been hurt worst by Ottawa's failure to bring rising prices under control.
Quebec also sent a telegram on June 25. There was an immediate response from right across the country which is being re-echoed by all speakers in the House at the present time. The minister of social affairs, the Hon. Claude E. Forget, of the Quebec Government sent a telegram in the following words:
First of all, I deplore the unilateral ceiling put on medical insurance by the federal government without warning-
There was absolutely no consultation. It was an arbitrary and a unilateral invasion of the provincial field. The quotation continues:
One must make the distinction between an economic measure favouring the Quebec taxpayer and an economic measure destined to advantage nothing but the federal treasury-the statement by (your) government belongs to this second category.
The federal government's hesitation in assuming its part of the financing of health services, in view of the present acts and agreements, shows once again how right Quebec is in favouring a fiscal transfer (of tax points) that would make the total financing responsibility coincide with the provinces complete responsibility in administering these services.
I could go on to quote from other statements by provincial ministers at the Victoria conference. Their objection and protest was universal, without exception, including the Liberal provincial administration. The Hon. Bill Mac-Eachen minister of public health, at the Victoria conference said:
I share a good deal of the concern of my colleagues from other provinces on the announcements made by the Hon. John Turner-
If I might interpolate again, now that the bill is before us, I am sure he would be even more forthright in his protestations. So we have a government which consistently over the last eight years has followed the divisive course of confrontation rather than co-operative federalism. It has continued on this course which is dangerous to national unity in-and I go back to the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs-the most important area of political health of the nation, by arbitrarily moving in this way.
We will have a return to the old, basic problem of confederation in which the rich provinces will be able to opt out because of their financial resources, while the poor provinces will have to reduce the level of their medical services. The regional disparities will be exacerbated. This is one of the main reasons the government, in introducing the universality of the program in 1968, said that in some provinces the people were poorly served because they did not have adequate financial resources, whereas in the well-to-do provinces they had adequate medical service. This bill will take us backward into that unhappy situation of regional disparity.
There has been some attempt to blame the doctors for the rising cost of health care. This point has been made before, but I should like to touch briefly on it today. It has been mentioned during the debate as the main problem in respect of the rising cost of medical care. I shall in a moment be putting forward some suggestions for solutions
Medical Care Act
in this regard. I wish now to come to the defence of the medical profession in Canada, because I think we are well served by our medical doctors and the people in the paramedical services.
I bring this particular point into the debate because of the difficulty that has been experienced in Manitoba in respect of the income of doctors in the past two months. There was a doctors' strike in my city of Brandon. For the first time, a professional group, the medical profession, paraded-with sandwich-boards-in front of the provincial hospital in that city. We were close to having another withdrawal of service, as the doctors were negotiating with the province of Manitoba for fair consideration of their salary position. The government started to blame the doctors for the inflationary costs in respect of medicine.
Let me put some figures on the record. If we say that the average income of a doctor is $50,000 per annum-and this is not excessive, in light of the salaries paid senior civil servants, and perhaps the attitude of the government in this regard is responsible for the inflationary pressure of salary demands among professionals-and there are some
36,000	physicians in Canada, the national gross income of physicians is approximately $1.17 billion. This means that each doctor would pay approximately $9,600 in federal taxes. This would represent a total of $346.5 million. If we look at the total of the federal transfer payments to the provinces in respect of medicare in 1974, we will find that the income tax paid by doctors amounted to 51 per cent of the total federal payment to the provincial governments.
The obvious attempt to place responsibility on the medical profession is a devious and irresponsible act on the part of the government. This problem did not come upon us suddenly: governments at the federal and provincial level have been wrestling with it for some time. The former minister of health, the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), initiated a task force on the cost of health services. That task force came up with three conclusions: one, that we could deal with it by reducing the standard of medical care-which we do not want to do in Canada-or we could increase taxes. Goodness knows, that has been going on in any event and we now are to have a further increase of 18 per cent in federal fiscal expenditures, which indicates that we are off into the stratosphere of financial irresponsibility. No wonder the Auditor General, in his report last year, said that federal financing is out of control completely. This is being confirmed as the committee dealing with the Auditor General's report deals with some of the examples of an irresponsible financial policy on the part of the federal government. Taxes have been raised and still they are not enough to meet the rising cost of government.
The third was the positive approach which has not been tried and which is regarded as the second stage of the health program in Canada. Ways and means must be found to keep down costs, and this is the point that I would like to deal with for a few moments before I conclude my remarks. There must be an initiative on the part of the federal government in achieving ways and means to keep down the costs, and there must be co-ordination among the provinces. Only the federal government is able to deal with this program on the basis of co-operative federalism, rather
11214

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
than confrontationist federalism. It is not good enough to put arbitrary ceilings on fiscal contributions to change the 50-50 formula which lured unsuspecting provincial governments into the program back in 1968. It is not good enough merely to dump the program on the provinces and tell them they have to solve it. This is precisely what Bill C-68 does.
First, I should like to deal with hospital care because it has been the worst offender. There are various ways of cutting the costs of hospital care which have never been implemented by any federal or provincial government up to the present time. We must have standards of hospital admission; this is now recognized by people in the health field. In fact, the Ontario government is busy setting up agencies throughout Ontario which would be able to deal with the problem of establishing standards for hospital admission. Ontario, rather than being criticized, should be complimented. I am sorry the hon. member for Broadview is not here, because they have pioneered in so many areas of health care in Canada that they should be receiving plaudits, not brick-bats, today.
The second area where costs should be cut is the length of bed occupancy. There is a great reluctance by patients to leave hospital once they have been able to obtain a bed, and many people in Canada have to wait weeks and even months to obtain a bed, particularly a surgical bed. Modern surgery does not agree to support the tendency present in all illness toward the invalid's complex, but prefers to get them moving and up and about as quickly as possible. So the length of bed occupancy must be taken into consideration.
The third item that could be dealt with in reducing the cost of hospital care is a review of the comprehensiveness of the medical care program. For example, should cosmetic surgery be covered under medicare? Should people who want their face lifted, for example, Madam Speaker, in order to improve their good looks, be covered under medicare? Yet this can be covered under the terms of reference as the program exists at present.
We have not begun to explore the possible savings under the home-visiting care plan. As a matter of fact, the patient recovers much more rapidly during the convalescent period in a happy home environment than he does in the sterile atmosphere of some of our hospitals. Even though the nurses are pretty, I am sure patients would find a much happier atmosphere in the home under a home-visiting care plan. Then we should do something about the provision of less costly convalescent beds. There is no necessity, during the convalescent period, to have all the costly resources of a modern hospital available. The convalescent period is merely biding one's time until he or she is able to return home and to their place of business and occupation.
Institutional care is most costly. I have been concerning myself with this matter with respect to the severely disabled and the chronically ill. I am the chairman of the Canadian Council for the Disabled which is engaged in a positive and constructive program of providing technical aids, adequate accommodation, transportation and accessibility to public buildings so that the severely disabled and the chronically ill can be assisted, some of them even to find useful and remunerative occupations. Certainly the chronically ill should be cared for in their own homes if

they have the support of the home-visiting care service and some of the marvellous technical aids that are now available.
We should look at the increasing cost of diagnostic services. Another incomprehensible approach which the government is taking to the rising cost of health care is their cut-backs in funds for medical research. This is one area where the problems of major illnesses could be resolved. If it were not for funds accumulated from private contributions, the whole program of cancer research would be severely hobbled. The same with heart disease. This is Heart Fund Week, if I am correct, and hundreds of thousands of dollars will be raised in order to come up with a solution for the rising cost of heart disease.
Every year, 10,000 males between the age of 40 and 60 are cut off in the prime of life by reason of coronary heart disease. I almost joined the ranks myself a few months ago, so I know whereof I speak. This is a cost to the economy of Canada which is astronomical, and it is one of the major reasons for the uncontrollable rising costs of health care in this country. Yet the government is cutting back on its research grants.
Here is another interesting situation. Our whole lifestyle, instead of contributing to a sound and healthy mind and body is based upon the pursuit of affluence which negates the best rules and regulations in health care. As someone who has gone through heart surgery and has to follow a very rigid diet, I am astonished to find that it is almost impossible to follow the required diet in restaurants. I was glad to hear the president of the Canadian Restaurant Association recently criticizing the restaurants of Canada for their failure to provide a diet which would support the urgent demand for better health care through a more common sense life-style for Canadians.
We have the problem of drug abuse and the problem of alcohol abuse which is one of the major areas of illness in Canada. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has made noises about doing something about the rising incidence of alcoholism which is now causing much concern in the province of Ontario and other provinces as well where they hope to lower the legal age for the consumption of alcohol from 21 years of age to 18.
The Health League of Canada is a voluntary organization which has been headed by that enthusiastic crusader for many years-ever since I came into the House of Commons-Dr. Gordon Bates. We used to have an active branch of this league in the House of Commons. It was supported by some of our MD colleagues; but we have not been as active in recent years as we should have been. However, this is the sort of positive approach we should be taking to bring down the rising costs of medicare and hospital care by positive preventive programs rather than by being content with merely providing a financial support system which was the first and urgent requirement of adequate health care. But now we must move to the second stage, and that is to implement programs which will cut down escalating costs.
In concluding, I should perhaps mention some more positive ideas for the government in its state of somnambulance these days. It does not seem to be able to come up
February 24, 1976

with very many constructive and creative ideas, so perhaps we can feed a few to it. The government should consider the motion which has been moved by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) for a six months' hoist. Perhaps that recommendation will be accepted. Certainly, the government should accept the recommendation which has been put forward by many speakers of the official opposition that something more positive and constructive must be implemented rather than merely shoving the blame and the responsibility on the provinces.
Here is one idea: recognizing the importance of financial control of the delivery of health services, it is proposed that a new financial partnership relationship with the provinces, in which the responsibility to manage and effectively to control these costs would be turned over to the provinces, where it belongs. Imperative to this policy decision will be an appropriate transfer of fiscal responsibilities through negotiated appropriate tax point transfers. At the same time, the provinces should allow constructive, co-ordinated entry by the Government of Canada into affairs of major concern on national health problems. I admit that the only way you can get an idea of this kind to operate is to have close co-operation and consultation, which has been the practice up until recent months in Canada.
A second proposal: for the serious Canadian health problems of mental health and drug and alcohol abuse it is proposed that a working partnership with the provinces and the professional agencies should be set up so we can quickly come to grips with these problems which are growing apace the longer we fail to deal with them. Third, with provincial acceptance and support, the Government of Canada should launch a new, all-encompassing research program under which biological and medical research, particularly in the areas of cancer and heart disease, would be intensified. As I have already indicated, instead of moving forward the government is moving backward in this regard.
Fourth, we must recognize that much research work must be done in the neglected areas of life-style and environmental health which contribute substantially to unacceptable disease levels. It would be my expectation that a national health research institute would represent a significant, well-balanced approach toward resolution of this problem. A fifth proposal would be that the federal government develop programs of prevention or education to alter the poor Canadian life-style habits as they contribute to the evolution of tragic and often fatal disease processes. In some cases, legislative intervention and action are requested to enhance healthy life-style habits. We have done this with regard to smoking. We hesitate to do it with regard to alcohol even though the minister has threatened to do so. I wish he would become active rather than merely speaking about the problem.
Sixth, governmental responsibility is supreme in the field of environmental factors affecting health. In the discussion of environmental health, specific courses of action should be taken by the government. Seventh, it is proposed that more appropriate participation by Canadian consumers in the future evolution of health policy be made by making public representation mandatory in a national institute for mental health and alcohol and drug abuse.
Medical Care Act
The voluntary Health League of Canada has been doing a marvellous task with its limited resources. Now the government must give support.
Finally, as I said at the opening of my remarks, this is a sad and unhappy debate. There is much unhappiness and uncertainty in the country because of the failure of this government to provide the necessary responsible and creative leadership. There is an old proverb which says that a merry heart doeth good like medicine. I think the best thing that could happen to this country would be a change of government so that Canadians could have a little bit of happiness for a change, and the health of Canadians would improve as a result.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who made many very constructive suggestions about how we could improve our health care, I sincerely hope that many of these suggestions are taken seriously by the government and considered carefully. I also listened to the speech of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert). I recognize his concern and take note of the motion he moved to give the bill a six-month hoist in order that the provinces can look into this matter more thoroughly. At the outset of my remarks with regard to Bill C-68 I should like to quote from the minister's preface to the book, "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians", as follows:
Good health is the bedrock on which social progress is built. A nation of healthy people can do those things that make life worth while, as the level of health increases so does the potential for happiness.
I am sure few people would dispute the advantages to be gained by encouraging individuals to pursue activities aimed at reducing health hazards and increasing health awareness among all Canadians. Preventive measures must be strengthened and people urged to become more health conscious and to assume more responsibility for their own physical well-being.
This is an issue which has always been of great concern to me, and as a relatively new member of parliament, in November of 1973 I moved a motion that in the opinion of the House the government should give consideration to the sponsorship and financing of a national recreation policy, in conjunction with the provinces and municipalities, to the allocation of responsibilities for recreational programming, to the determination of land use and to the encouragement of all aspects of recreational development by local citizens under permanent, federally-assisted programs. You can appreciate my pleasure when the government introduced its working document.
The government should provide us with health care. It is under an obligation, to the citizens of this country, to introduce programs and facilities which will make people aware of the detrimental effects on health of lack of exercise, improper diet, the consumption of excessive amounts of alcohol, and the smoking of cigarettes. I emphasize that all this should come under one comprehensive program and not under haphazard programs, as is the case at present. Present programs lead to much duplication of work in certain areas.
21419-18V2

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
It seems paradoxical that this bill should have been introduced at the present time, a bill that will have the potential for doing irreparable, major damage to the quality of medical care and Canada's medical insurance program, particularly in have-not provinces which do not operate with large budgets. Surely a program promoting increased health awareness should work in conjunction with a cohesive, beneficial medical insurance scheme. Preventive measures are much desired, and undoubtedly in the long run will serve to decrease the cost of health services. But we must also ensure that comprehensive, high quality services will continue to be available to all eligible residents of Canada.
I emphasize the point made by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk). It is totally illogical and unreasonable to freeze the Medical Research Council program. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris also mentioned this. Only with increased research and study of health problems and solutions thereto can the over-all health standard of all citizens be raised.
Canada's medical system has a fine reputation in the world. We have every right to be proud of a plan which has worked well, proved responsive, and demonstrated that it can work to the advantage of all citizens. Now it seems that the primary object of the program, the provision of health care to all Canadians, is to be sacrificed and tailored to financial exigencies of the moment rather than to medical care requirements. This policy naturally poses a major threat to the health of all Canadians.
Of utmost importance is the fact that the government has made a totally arbitrary, unilateral decision to impose budgetary ceilings on health care expenditures. The reaction of the provinces criticizing the government for its inflexibility, unilateral action, and arbitrariness in this matter is real and well founded. The need to reduce costs and control spending during this period of high inflation is not to be questioned. On the other hand the lack of prior consultation with provinces, in an effort to bring about economies in health care, ought to be questioned.
A unilateral decision was made by the federal government, contrary to the recommendations of the 1969 task force report, which suggested that consultation should take place between provincial and federal levels of government before any monetary changes in the program are made or even considered. In addition we must remember that the entire present day medical health system was forced down the throats of the provinces against their wishes. Apparently the federal government wants to opt out, to limit its contribution to cost-sharing. Its action leaves many provinces out on a limb. Small wonder the provinces are bewildered, indignant, and unanimous in opposing this legislation.
One of the main reasons for the introduction of Bill C-68 is that the government says that the cost of maintaining the present system is becoming too great. The costs are becoming unwieldy. In the budget speech of last June the then minister of finance maintained that the cost of health care had risen 20 per cent over the last year. In essence that statement was correct, but the minister neglected to mention that most of the increase was the direct result of escalating expenditures in hospital, not medical, care. In the last two years for which figures are fully available,

1972-73 and 1973-74, medical costs rose by 9.2 per cent and 7.2 per cent respectively. As well, medical care costs have decreased as a proportion of gross national expenditure. They constitute a smaller percentage of gross national product. The obvious question is: why has the federal government arbitrarily established spending ceilings on a program which has not been plagued with the sort of runaway cost increases evident in other federally-sponsored projects?
The government argues that in view of the past record of the somewhat slow increase in medical costs, the proposed ceiling is really no ceiling at all. Although expenditures appear to be under relative control the possibility still exists that there could be a rapid upturn in the capital outlay required to maintain our health standards. Many provinces claim that they need a catch-up period in order to bring their regional standards up to national levels. Such being the case, a marked increase in medical care expenditures would become evident.
The bill does not ensure economies in medical care, the very purpose for which the government imposed the ceilings. Provinces may wish to improve their health services, and doctors may demand higher salaries. As others have said, doctors are paid no more than many civil servants. In the event that either of the two situations alluded to should occur, the provinces would bear the burden of the additional capital outlay. Necessarily, premium rates will increase, or provincial revenues will have to be depleted. The third possibility is that if the provinces cannot meet this budgetary constraint, medical services will have to be reduced.
Bill C-68 may well endanger the quality and availability of medical care for Canadians. Medical care may be rationed and the increased ceilings may inhibit if not prohibit the introduction of new medical procedures and render it impossible for them to be made accessible to many individuals who would benefit greatly from them.
Recently on a trip to Calgary I visited a hospital auxiliary unit-I think that is the correct term-and was shown a very impressive piece of equipment which the unit had acquired. The people of the locality had raised money for the Foothills Hospital. Actually I was surprised to learn how many people were involved in raising money for the project. They raised money for a machine which neither the federal nor provincial governments could afford to buy for the hospital, a machine which, using a computer, will be able to detect aneurisms. It was an expensive machine, which the people bought through their own efforts.
What will the bill do to the have not provinces? The effect will be particularly detrimental to such provinces whose less developed health care programs have truly benefited from the federal-provincial cost-sharing formula.
We condone improved health care cost efficiency and the control of health care cost escalation. Positive steps should and must be taken. It is time for federal government initiative in health reform, but this legislation as it now stands offers no reform at all. It merely passes the buck, as it were, to the provinces without offering anything concrete in return.
February 24, 1976

Instead of imposing statutory ceilings the government should establish them by regulation which would allow an annual examination and revision, which would ensure close federal budget monitoring while at the same time it would guarantee the desired level of health standards.
The concept of establishing a tripartite committee to explore all fiscal aspects of medical financing is one that has already been mentioned by hon. members on this side of the House. Such a committee, consisting of both provincial and federal representatives as well as members of the medical profession, would play an integral part in developing the regulatory guidelines.
In the sphere of general health and hospital care the federal government should suggest specific areas in which investigation respecting need and efficiency could be carried out in conjunction with the provinces-for example, examination of the standards of hospital admission, as recently reported in the press, the length of bed occupancy in hospitals, the use of X-ray and laboratory equipment in local clinics and hospitals and, as stated by my colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, the necessity of including cosmetic surgery under medicare.
To return to the point made earlier in my remarks, the escalation of a comprehensive health awareness program would prove invaluable to an eventual decrease of health care costs. The importance of regular physical examinations to detect and treat such irregularities as heart disease cannot be over-emphasized. It is unbelievable that some people do not have a physical examination once a year. They live for years with high blood pressure and do not know it.
Media campaigns such as that conducted by the government with regard to Participaction would be good. That campaign made people aware of their physical condition. It made me aware of it. I have a friend in my small town who is about 48 years of age. Every day he goes through an intensive physical program including jogging and various other exercises. When he asked me to join him on the track, I said that I would take him up on it. I was 27.

She can join me on the track any time.
Recently I have had conversations with physicians. I believe there are some duplications in their expensive equipment. One physician stated he believed that proper
Medical Care Act
equipment in centrally located hospitals is a necessity and that an ambulance ride of no more than 20 or 30 minutes would be adequate. As it is now some small hospitals feel it is necessary to have all this expensive equipment.
In summary, I recognize that we should try to curb or control health care costs. However, it is my opinion and that of my colleagues that the provisions of Bill C-68, while they may in the long-run serve this end, will undoubtedly be detrimental to the entire health care program and the purpose for which it was originally established. We have an excellent system in operation at the moment here in Canada, one highly regarded by other nations. Surely we must not jeopardize it by allowing this legislation to become law, but must instead seek other methods whereby health care cost efficiency can be increased, methods that will not be injurious but beneficial to the physical wellbeing of Canadians.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a number of years ago I would have thought it would be totally unnecessary for members of parliament to stand in this House and defend the type of medicare program we have enjoyed since 1968.
Years ago in Timmins, as a miner, I remember talking about the establishment of a health care plan for the miners in that area as the next stage in a form of insurance that then covered the miners with very limited medical service. In trying to sell the idea of a comprehensive plan for a limited number of people in a closed area, we met with violent reaction on the part of many people. There was to be a payment for this group health insurance.
The next stage was when I observed at some distance the province of Saskatchewan deciding to provide the citizens of that province with a group hospital insurance plan.
In 1968, the federal government introduced a program that was so advantageous that most provinces could not refuse to participate, even though they had never before been involved in such an extensive program. As the government was going to pay 50 per cent of their costs, they felt they had to go into the plan.
In several of the mining towns many of us had a group plan that we ourselves had operated for some years. At one time we had a doctor who lost his licence to practice because he had been guilty of procuring abortions. That doctor had been hired to assist in the operation of the plan. It was a very successful plan. But even after those years of participating in a comprehensive plan there was still violent reaction to everyone joining the Ontario plan.
It is interesting now to see the federal government trying to put on the brakes. Medical expenditures must be curtailed. This is being done by the federal government cutting down on its participation with the provinces. This is a backward step.
The federal government is doing one of two things, but has not stated which. It is either saying it is going to economise on the backs of the sick of the nation, or that the provinces should reduce the plans they have implemented because the federal government will not continue to make its contribution of 50 per cent. The federal government agreed in 1967-68 to continue to make a payment with

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
an increase in view, but now it suggests that over a five-year period it wishes to curtail expenditures in this field.
I do not believe the federal government wishes to take over medicare services in Canada. I doubt whether it would be well advised to do so.
I recall some of the silly remarks made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) which certainly did not enhance his reputation with me. I can remember when contaminated meat was being sold in certain parts of the country, and his suggestion was to cook it more. I suppose this was an old Biblical or pre-Biblical quotation, something in the Talmud, according to which people did not eat certain types of meat, including pork, because they carried pestilence and infection. Their use was totally banned.
It might be possible in a few years for the minister, if he is still the responsible minister at that time, to bring in a whole list of things we are not supposed to eat because they are cancer-causing. Perhaps we shall find ourselves confronted with a whole list of these things, including charcoal broiled steaks and other items which might have some effect on our health.
The strength of a nation will be judged according to its ability to provide itself with a number of basic services. One of these must be a health service. When the world was uncivilized, emerging from the caves, those who got along best were those who knew how to cure their wounds in a manner better than their neighbours, those who could make best use of certain types of herbs or natural remedies which they were able to find. The use they made of these skills determined their type of culture to a great extent.
If we look back into history we find there were people in the world a long time ago who had developed certain skills in medical treatment to a relatively high degree, and if we examine those cultures we find they were also able to develop almost all the other facets of their civilization somewhat in keeping with their ability to provide medical services. Thousands and thousands of years ago there were physicians who could carry out operations on the brain, operations to repair broken bones, and so on. In some cases apparently abdominal surgery was undertaken; gallbladders were removed and primitive heart surgery was performed. These civilizations must have been quite highly developed. Consider the Egyptian civilization and the preMexican civilization. Both had developed medical skills which enabled their people to move ahead faster than their neighbours.
It is interesting to reflect that our backward minister of health should hit out at reducing the money available for the development of health services. There is no doubt in my mind that the quality of health service across the nation is not consistent. Some people who live in Ontario's golden horseshoe suffer from restricted vision. If they cannot see a thing from the top of the new tower they have built in the city of Toronto, it doesn't exist. If they cannot see health services outside that area, they do not exist and therefore the people do not exist or, certainly, they are not entitled to the benefits available to those who live in the metropolitan area. What is happening in Ontario is only the beginning of what will happen across the nation.

The provinces came into the scheme in many cases because they found it impossible to carry the total burden of providing adequate care for their people. Maybe it should not be mentioned, but there used to be a joke in the Armed Forces that if you went to one particular province you had only to buy a girl a set of false teeth and she would be your friend for life. Where that type of service is not available in a province it should be our responsibility, the responsibility of all Canadians, to provide it. Some of the provinces which are not as wealthy as the central provinces will be forced to cut down further in their provision of essential services.
It always amazes me-and I have said this to the Ontario minister of health-that we should be building new hospitals in some areas only to find, after three of four weeks of operation, on visiting those hospitals there are seven or eight beds out in the corridors. If we cannot plan far enough ahead to guess what is likely to happen in seven or eight weeks there must be something wrong with the type of planning we are doing.
We are experiencing a spot of trouble in Kirkland Lake at the present time. I am not referring to one of the hospitals they are going to close, though they did close the big hospital-parts of it were only 12 years old; they did so with the intention of building the new hospital, one which is considerably smaller. The old hospital had beds in the corridors. And again, in the new, small hospital, there are patients in the corridors.
I talked to the director of hospitals in Ontario and it was interesting to hear him say that 20 beds had been set aside for chronic care. There are hospitals in Florida where it costs $2,000 to stay. Kirkland Lake is cheap by those standards. I spent a few weeks in hospital in Ottawa and it cost well over $100 a day. It is a lot cheaper at Kirkland Lake, at $84. But it would be cheaper still to keep those people in a chronic care unit. That way you could keep three people for the price of one. May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before we adjourned for dinner I was pointing out that one of the difficulties in Ontario has been inability to adapt medicare to our hospital services in order to make full use of the facilities available and give the widest amount of health care in the most reasonable manner. I used the example of Kirkland Lake where a new hospital much smaller than the last has been built. A number of beds were set aside for chronic care patients; in fact almost one quarter of the hospital beds are allocated to such patients. The old hospital has been vacated. It is still owned and heated by the province and was very suitable for patients needing chronic care. This kind of care would considerably reduce medical costs. Yet we do not see fit to develop this kind of secondary service for patients who can be better cared for in chronic care hospitals. This kind of care makes less demands on surgical processes as it is a more residential type of care.
February 24, 1976

Closing hospitals in Ontario means that many persons will receive less care than previously. One of the matters of concern to the people of northern Ontario is that there is going to be a major change made in the northeastern psychiatric hospital. Ontario has never been very fair to the people in the northern part of the province so far as psychiatric care in this hospital is concerned. In my opinion this hospital was built as a monument to the representative of the area rather than as a centre providing psychiatric care. Nevertheless, it is a big facility and much better use could be made of it.
Consideration is now being given by the minister of health of Ontario to closing the facility and relocating the patients, using the hospital for some other purpose. Anyone who examines the development of that particular hospital will be made aware that we have never had adequate psychiatric care in that area. The hospital has been operated in the main by one psychiatrist, when they could have used seven or eight. The ancillary services required to operate this kind of hospital have been non-existent. People in the northeastern part of the province are well aware that the hospital may be used for some other purpose but feel it should continue to operate for the benefit of the people.
In addition to closing hospitals we are anticipating removal of the laboratory in North Bay. Although it is not a very big or important lab it is the place where specimens from my part of northern Ontario are sent. If the lab is closed it will mean these specimens will have to go to Toronto, or to a provincial lab in some other part of the province. The distance would be considerable and the process time consuming. The laboratory in North Bay has served a necessary function for the people of that area.
I believe the minister of health has traded off the health of the residents of Canada for money. He has traded off this kind of health care for a return of only $50 million. I am sure most Canadians believe that we in this nation are able to afford not reduced medicare but expanded medicare.
It is a fact that at the present time our jails contain many persons who should not be in them. I am always amused when someone makes the charge that under our parole or temporary relief system a mentally incapable person has been released and that our system has not been able to prevent this. A large number of people in jails in Canada today are not receiving adequate medical attention or psychiatric care simply because we have failed to supply the trained personnel who can give them this kind of treatment. If we did more in this field we would be able to reduce the population in our penitentiaries.
This represents no small saving, Madam Speaker. It costs a minimum of $10,000 to keep one person in jail for one year in one of our federal institutions. It would not require too many to use up the kind of return the minister is going to get from curtailing medical services.
This is also true in the field of drugs. I have been very interested in learning of some of the sentences that have been handed out in regard to drug abuse in the last two or three years. There is a tendency on the part of judges to be lenient with many of those who are not habitual drug users, or even with those who have been convicted more than once of selling drugs. I suspect this is because of one
Medical Care Act
very simple fact, namely, if they are drug addicts of any kind and put into our jail system they receive absolutely no rehabilitative assistance. We have established very few half-way houses and very few centres directed toward curing some of these problems in our drug communities.
It seems to me the minister should be very interested in going into these fields and areas in which our young people have been affected so alarmingly in the last number of years. We have failed in many ways to provide the type of medical care we should be providing. It is wrong for the minister to say now that we are not going to meet the 50 per cent the provinces are willing to put up for the medicare programs they have established, and are not going into any additional programs or allow the provinces to go into them unless they finance them themselves.
While it is true that Ontario has a Conservative and probably a reactionary government, it is also true that other provinces will be going down the same road toward reducing medical costs because of an inability to meet added expenditures. There may well be some provinces that will make a contribution from the provincial treasury to develop or extend programs that are already in existence where there is an obvious demand for and an interest in those programs. Many of these efforts will be made in respect of those fields where people are not able to look after themselves. I suspect these efforts will be made in the psychiatric field, in respect of juvenile offenders, and in respect of the elderly. Provinces will have to face the difficulty of providing for those who cannot be cared for at home and who have to be institutionalized in one way or another.
The charge has been made that we are again establishing the idea of penalizing those who use medical services. I was always impressed by the argument put forward by a Liberal member many years ago when talking about automobile insurance. I think this argument applies equally as well to the medicare insurance program. He said he had driven an automobile for 20 or 30 years, never had an accident and had never collected one red cent from the insurance company, but that did not mean he did not believe in automobile insurance. It just meant he was fortunate enough not to have had to take advantage of the insurance for which he was paying the premium. I think that is true of medicare as well.
Those who are well surely do not object to making a contribution to the medicare scheme of this nation in order to cover all Canadians, even though they may feel they may never receive any benefit from the medicare program. This would only indicate that they expect never to be seriously ill or suffer from a lengthy sickness. Canadians generally have not made the decision to curtail medicare services. The general trend has been in the other direction.
There is great sympathy and support in all communities for the developement of day-care centres, schools for young children who have serious learning problems, and schools for young children with hypertension problems. There is a great deal of support for the establishment of schools to provide for slow learners, those hard of hearing and others suffering from all kinds of difficulties, particularly those that mainly affect young people. Much of this

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
support comes from the educational system at the local level, supported by the communities, because the local people are knowledgeable and concerned about the welfare of those less fortunate than themselves.
It is wrong for the minister to assume that the people of Canada do not want to extend the medicare scheme. It is irresponsible to suggest that the federal government should no longer contribute toward the extension of medicare shemes but should curtail welfare programs and their extension. The increase of 13 per cent allowed under this measure is not sufficient to meet even the increase in population. It will not in the first year meet the anticipated population growth nor the increase in demand for health services. This means we will be worse off unless the provinces contribute more than their 50 per cent share.
I should like to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare pay more attention to some of the recommendations in the Hall report. I should like to see him bring before parliament some indication from his officials that studies had been conducted which would indicate there are alternatives to the curtailment of medical services in Canada. There are other curtailments that would allow for the same or increased medical services. One might be in the form of deterrent fees, while another might be in the form of more efficient supervision within the hospital structure. It may be there are certain types of cosmetic operations that could be eliminated from the plan. There are a number of possible alternatives which would allow the minister to contribute a 50 per cent share of a universal medicare scheme for all Canadians, thus providing the kind of health services that we living in this society demand.
I was impressed by those hon. members who said during this debate that they were shocked by the minister taking pride in the fact that Canada ranks fifth or sixth in the provision of health services in the world.

speechtext: We are first.

speechtext: Maybe I am being parochial, but I think we should be first. I have been in other countries and observed health care services there, and I know we are not first. speechtext: Even red Tories.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Any kind, left, right or centre. I am not surprised that Conservatives are joining us in this attempt to have the minister change his mind about reductions in this field. A long time ago I heard an interesting definition of a Conservative, and I was interested in comparing that definition to the one I heard used on television in the last few days.
An old gentleman told me years ago that a Conservative was a man who fights all his life to retain what his father fought all his life to prevent. I can remember Conservatives fighting very hard a number of years ago to see that medicare was not brought into being in Canada. Now they are fighting very hard to retain it in its present form. I

congratulate them for that. I sincerely believe that if there is any field to which the government should give consideration it is the field of providing and extending medical care services to the people.
I do not think it is possible to equate money with people's lives. I do not think we can have a healthy population if people live in unsanitary or unsuitable accommodation. I do not believe it is possible to have a healthy nation when 10 per cent or 12 per cent of the population is continually unemployed, nor do I think we can have a healthy nation when we do not provide, to the best of our ability, adequate health service to all the people. I do not think we have been providing it to the best of our ability. I believe much more could be done.
I am quite sure we should be spending ten times the amount we spend on research. I am always shocked to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare make statements such as we now have a report from the United States saying that cyclamates are cancer-forming and that they will have to be withdrawn. We do not have any research people in Canada capable of making such a decision. We have to hear about it from the Americans. This is the reason sometimes we make a mistake in taking an item off the market and then finding we have to put it back on the market again. We have not reached the stage where we can conduct our own research in respect of food additives and so on. We do not have the research facilities and qualified staff to provide this service.
I found it interesting to hear that while there is a shortage of blood in Canada the Red Cross can sell it internationally. Now it seems we are wondering whether the blood we are sending to other countries meets our standards. I understand there is some question about this.
We hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare tell the Canadian people that hamburger is bad, that it is horse meat or that it comes from dead animals. It is suggested that it contains a large amount of bacteria but that if it is cooked for another five minutes it will not have any bad effect. If that is the kind of advice our federal Department of Health provides the Canadian people then we have not progressed too far and we are not spending too much money on the health of our nation. I think the priorities of the government are wrong.
There is no doubt in my mind that if the government wishes to curtail services in a number of fields one of these fields is the civil service. It is obviously top heavy. I have heard that there is a cut-back in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. They are not cutting back those at the top but are cutting back on the number of Indians who have been hired by the Department. That is par for the course.
There are cuts which can be made in Canada, but there are some fields in which I do not think we should compromise. Certainly health must be one of the fields in which curtailment of service is neither desirable nor feasible if we are to have a strong and healthy nation.
I was very interested to listen to the, I presume, 27-year old member this afternoon when he indicated that when he was 26 years old he could not run around a quarter mile track more than once. I am pleased to learn that he has

taken unto himself a training program that will provide fitness. I think this is a very good idea. It is something we should be looking at with a view to encouraging the Canadian people to exercise and take advantage of what I consider to be preventive measures which up to date we in this country have not taken much pain to promote.
I remember hearing the previous minister of national health and welfare talk about giving up smoking. It was supposed to be bad for the lungs and cancer-producing. But while he was lecturing the Canadian people his cigarette smoke was flying in all directions. I do not see the present minister engaging in athletic activities that would encourage our young people to follow his example. Certainly when we come back from an international series of games with only one gold medal it is obvious that we are not as developed in the athletic sense as are some other countries.
It is interesting to note that in most European countries the people engage in calisthenics and active sport from an early age, not for the purpose of beating up each other as we do in some of our sports but in order to gain athletic prowess so that the nation will have healthy people who will maintain their health in the years to come. I speak not from experience but from observation. I have reached the age at which people have heart attacks and all the other things. Since I left manual labour some years ago I certainly have not followed the kind of advice I advocate. However, there has been very little leadership given in this field.

I think this would be one of the most important things the Canadian parliament could do for some time to come.
I believe it is absolutely necessary that all members of parliament speak out against this unreasonable reduction. I rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker. The hon. member has spoken quite a bit about hospitals. This bill deals with medical care. It has nothing to do with hospital insurance. It has nothing to do with whatever the
Medical Care Act
minister of health for Ontario is doing in respect of hospitals. I submit discussion of hospital costs and hospital insurance is outside the scope of the bill we are debating.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
The Canadian people have now witnessed very plainly exactly why we are not satisfied with the Minister of National Health and Welfare or with the bill which is before us. He does not see any relationship between hospitals and medical care. I do not know where he thinks the money comes from in Ontario for the medical care aspect. I wonder whether we would have all the doctors and support staff we have if operations were to be carried out on someone's kitchen table.
Hospitals are part of the package. They are not financed by the federal government, but obviously if you rob Peter you will have to get it from Paul, or from Mark, to retain the biblical flavour. It would seem to me that the minister of health in Ontario, the same as every minister of health in Canada, is limited to the amount of money which he has available for health services in that province. If he has to pay more to medicare, he will have tq take it from the hospital care budget because it will have to be a package deal and the money has to come from somewhere.
If the Minister of National Health and Welfare does not know that, then I feel sorry for him, but I am more sorry for the provincial ministers of health with whom he has to deal. If he can divide it up among them, I am sorry for them because it will not be possible for them to get what they need when they go to their respective cabinets and ask for their allotment. This has produced some very bad results in Ontario, and I think it will produce bad results all across the country. I am worried that this is likely to get progressively worse.
This legislation does not take into consideration an escalator clause in the cost of living which would normally be expected, and it does not take into consideration the population growth. These are fixed considerations which remain year after year. The criterion should be that as we increase in wealth in Canada, and as our gross national product and our productivity increase, we should be able to supply more medicare services to Canadians, not less.
