subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
May I say, Madam Speaker, that I have followed this debate with great interest. Unfortunately, I have not been here for most of the speeches, but I have read them carefully and I think the majority of points have been made in this debate. However, there are a few issues with which I would like to deal for a few minutes this evening. Let me say at the outset that I believe this piece of legislation before us, in particular in view of the announcement by the former minister of finance in June that there would be renegotiation of the Hospital Diagnostic Services Act at a later date, is perhaps the most regressive legislation that I have seen introduced in the House since 1972.
I have no intention of repeating the various figures that have been supplied by many hon. members throughout this

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
debate. They indicate in fact that the cost of the medicare program has been below the projected figures in the past two or three years.
I have no hesitation in supporting the suggestions that have been made that we need a far more flexible arrangement between the provinces and the federal government so that we can have programs which will permit the development of either comparable or better services at a lower cost.
I have no intention this evening of entering into the numbers game, but I submit that if any province were forced by this legislation to find additional sums of money to implement the program, the obvious winner of course would be the federal government. Let me give as an example, say, the province of Ontario. I think it is quite obvious that if this bill were introduced and passed and the provincial government found it necessary to find, speaking hypothetically, $100 million to service that program and they were taxed at the rate of approximately 50 per cent, it takes little imagination and a very dull pencil to figure out who would be the benefactor.
What concerns me about this bill is that it is obviously a political struggle between the provinces and the federal government, and I believe it is at the expense of the health care system and would involve the entire social security system in Canada. I was very interested in the minister's comments when he made his speech. He found it necessary to defend this bill, particularly following the inception of the anti-inflation program which, to the casual observer, should have made this bill somewhat obsolete. I could not help but recall an article in one of the Ottawa newspapers of June 26 written by Richard Gwyn. What he said is probably coming true. He wrote:
The sharpest pre-budget debate pitted Turner against welfare minister Marc Lalonde, the minister best able to match him on even terms. Turner wanted hospital and medical services costs curbed: Lalonde argued for his own projects, and lost. The score between these cabinet heavyweights now is Turner two, Lalonde one. Earlier this year Turner got the starting date for Lalonde's guaranteed income plan postponed, but Lalonde came back later to win cabinet approval to make a financial offer to the provinces.
I think that a good deal of the negotiations that have taken place between the federal and provincial authorities are known to us in a general way. Many of us on this side of the House who are extremely interested in the entire social security program are somewhat concerned that greater details are not available to us, not only with reference to the medicare program-I know the minister was talking about this somewhat earlier-but with reference to the total security program, because this is in fact part of that parcel.
During his speech on January 28 of this year the minister was discussing ways and means of controlling health costs and he made reference to his working document "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians". He emphasized preventive methods and the necessity of people assuming more responsibility for monitoring and improving their health. He also emphasized the necessity of reducing health hazards in the environment. I have no difficulty in identifying with the minister's comments, and indeed I myself have spoken on these issues and on the necessity of redirecting our resources within the health

care system to achieve some of the goals the minister has mentioned.
The minister knows that I approve of the approach in principle in terms of the health policy, and particularly in terms of the cornerstones of this policy when he talks about lifestyles, environmental components, the health care organization, and human biology. I think it does permit a more rational and rapid method of analysing health policies, somewhat better than the traditional breakdown we have seen in the past, when we talk about such things as preventive or rehabilitative medicine and when we talk about mental health, public health, diagnostic services, a multitude of terms used in the past. There is no question that this formula which has been talked about in the past, and which I have written about, certainly rationalizes the health care system to a greater degree than has been experienced in the past.
It also has the advantage of emphasizing the preventive side of health care as opposed to the more traditional curative side about which we frequently talk.
What I object to is that the minister has utilized the working paper as a smoke screen to justify the introduction of this bill. He has really not provided an adequate forum for an adequate debate, and indeed has not provided leadership in translating these words in the past year or two into action. I must emphasize to the minister that the health field concept as visualized in his working document raises far more questions than answers. Surely he must realize that the literature is filled with articles which emphasize the prevention of diseases, articles which discuss the promotion of health, and articles dealing specifically with various areas of health education, and there is no doubt that this emphasis is relevent to our current and future needs.
However, the reality of the situation is that the record thus far has not been impressive, and the minister knows that the curative bias we see in our health care system will not magically disappear in the near future, and of course will have little impact in terms of the cost which the minister would like us to believe will occur with this particular concept.
I have no intention of embarking on a philosophical discussion at this particular time as to the extent government should be involved, whether it be in environmental matters or lifestyle matters. I think this is an important debate which should take place at some point in time, but I caution the minister to assess it very carefully-and I suggest that he should have a complete understanding of the implications of this particular document he has presented on a health perspective. The risk is not in the concept, but the risk and the danger are that the concept may be misinterpreted or misused, and in the final analysis if that were to occur, it would then fail because of lack of understanding.
I believe the minister is attempting to mislead us by employing this health concept which he has introduced and by saying that savings are available; yet we know that there is not adequate statistical or epidemiological data at this time to make certain that these concepts will surely work and will surely be effective. I think it is very impor-
February 24, 1976

tant at some future date that we do have the statistical data and that we do have the epidemiological studies which are required before some of these particular decisions are made, or before governments embark on very grandiose programs which could be very costly and perhaps of little help.
There are many features of the working document and the concept which should be debated, but by way of illustration I should like briefly to look at two examples which I think would point out very clearly the lack of interest of the minister in the particular concept, or perhaps his lack of understanding of the concept, in areas in which he and the government could move in a more positive fashion.
The minister quite rightly emphasized throughout his speech the importance of the industrial safety program, and he specifically made reference to the program called LIFE, "learn industrial first aid effectively," a program which is carried out by that very superb group, the St. John Ambulance Society. However, it is more relevant to ask the minister what comprehensive program he and his department have developed in terms of industrial safety and in terms of occupational hazards. Just for a moment let me mention, for example, words like mercury poisoning, Minamata's disease, arsenic poisoning, lead poisoning and radiation poisoning. These are terms common to the tongues of all individuals. I suggest if there is an area where there is need and where federal leadership could be demonstrated in terms of environmental and lifestyle problems, surely this is such an area.
I suggest that at his first opportunity the minister present to this House his comprehensive document, if he has it, which would clearly define the policy of the government in terms of dealing with occupational hazards and safety standards, to which he referred in his speech in January.
Let me give one final example in this regard and refer to the minister's insincerity. Perhaps that is a little too harsh. I will refer to his lack of understanding of the health field concept which he has proposed. I now refer to that important concept referred to as the area of human biology. Yet if one reads his speech very carefully there is no reference to that particular cornerstone of the health field concept about which he has talked. I think it is important to understand why this was left out of the minister's speech.
Certainly since I came to the House in 1972 the minister has demonstrated very clearly that he has little or no interest in the field of medical research. I must admit that at one point after a great deal of effort in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs there was a supplementary estimate, as the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) pointed out in his speech, in which there was a freezing of funds for medical research within the past two years.
If we look at the definition of human biology, it deals principally with that area which applies to applied and pure research. Of course it also implies the implementation of measures to combat diseases which are genetic in origin or related to human biology. I think this is extremely important. As a matter of fact, if I may, I should like to quote an article from the Canadian Medical Association Journal of September, 1974, entitled "constitutional impasse has impeded health dialogue." I believe this article
Medical Care Act
is as pertinent today as it was at that time. It relates to the entire area of medical research and was combined, actually, with the whole area of research at the time. If I may say so, I wrote this article in September of 1974.
However, I think it is relevant because in my view the minister again has ignored this particular problem which is part of his health field concept. I think this represents an attitude on the part of the minister and the federal government in the entire field of health. I should like to quote as follows:
With the advent of universal hospital and medical coverage we have witnessed a rapid escalation of health costs and the inevitable platitudes demanding a more efficient, comprehensive and co-ordinated health care system.
The inability to resolve the constitutional and fiscal responsibilities for health care at federal-provincial conferences has created an era of paralysis in dealing with health problems that are national in scope. Research, education and health care are the victims of this paralysis. Medical research typifies an important building block of our health care system that is seriously threatened by recent actions of the federal government.
The decrease of funds in constant dollars to the Medical Research Council has created a crisis situation in the biomedical research community. The sweeping changes proposed for Canadian science in the throne speech in February have added to the uncertainty of the future role and importance of medical research. These changes and the absence of clearly defined objectives have produced instability and scepticism in many areas of science.
The Medical Research Council, as an autonomous crown corporation, has been the agency responsible for the major allocation of federal support towards medical research. Successive budgets of the Medical Research Council and the Department of National Health and Welfare reveal a significant change in attitude, if not policy, towards medical research.
During the late 60's, there was an expansion of the medical Research Council's budget augmented by the Health Resources Fund. The budgets reflected the need and desire to create a viable and effective Canadian health research community. The confidence experienced during that era and the hope for the future were the needed stimuli to attract scientists and provide career opportunities for young qualified students.
In contrast to the late 60's, the budgets of the Medical Research Council during the 70's have seen a decline in constant dollar spending, a rejection of excellent research, cuts in personnel support programs and an increase in terminal grants. This has been accompanied by an increase of funds from the Department of National Health and Welfare for the National Health Grants Program established in 1970 to promote research into health care and the health care delivery systems, and an increase in expenditures for the non-medical use of drugs program. This shift in policy by the federal government has occurred at the expense of biomedical research and without an appreciation of the interdependence of all health research programs.
The science policy announced in the throne speech-
And the announcement was extremely important.
-constitutes substantial and significant changes that will undoubtedly have far-reaching effects in public policy. The scope and authority of the Ministry of State, Science and Technology ... are to be broadened and strengthened to such an extent it will have the potential of a superministry virtually affecting every scientific endeavour in Canada.
The proposed changes will involve government structures and future policy orientation and development. Thousands of the most able and highly qualified people in the country, together with the teaching and research institutions across Canada, will be directly affected. With the appropriation of hundreds of millions of dollars at its disposal every year, the total spectrum of research and development will be directly related to government priorities and national goals.
Germane to the future of medical research is the proposed re-orientation of the Medical Research Council. The council will report to the

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
government through the Minister of State for Science and Technology as will the two proposed new granting councils, the Natural Science Research Council and a Social Science and Humanities Research Council. These councils will be co-ordinated by an intercouncil co-ordinating committee chaired by the secretary of MOSST and will report to the Minister of State for Science and Technology.
In the vernacular of the politician we have been assured that the Medical Research Council will remain unchanged ...
This, as we know, is nonsense.
... The council is now to relate to government through a science and technology ministry; this is significant in that it will in time result in substantial changes in its function. In addition, the throne speech announcements signal new directions in government research policy and the decision by the government that the work of the various research councils and granting bodies should more directly serve its own policy objectives.
In the relatively short span of eight years, the prestigious Medical Research Council has seen a confident future replaced by financial crisis and the sanctity of autonomy founded and developed on the principle of scientific excellence threatened by internal reorganization. In addition, the Medical Research Council will be divorced from the expanding intramural and extramural research programs developed by the Department of National Health and Welfare, thereby severing the interdependence of health research, creating fragmentation.
This atmosphere of stagnation and ill-defined change has created new phenonema alien to many in the academic and research community and to the profession as a whole.
The funds for medical research have not kept pace with society's demands or the research community's expectations. There are increased difficulties in deciding to which discipline or project money should preferentially go. There is a growing feeling that the quality of the research people and the significance of their work is not recognized by the policymakers responsible for funding research. The controversy of pure versus applied research remains as a vestige of an earlier era, unresolved and ill-fitted within the framework of health care research.
The ultimate goal of all health research is to improve the health of each Canadian. Society expects-and we have the responsibility to ensure-high standards of medical education, health service and health care. Research is linked intimately to the training of professional manpower and a high-quality health care system is therefore dependent on a viable research base. Medical and health education, medical and health research and the health-care delivery system are inseparably linked.
To date there is not a national policy for medical research. The federal and provincial governments have not defined their plans and policies for health, health resources and health-care systems, nor have they indicated a policy and financial support to preserve and strengthen medical research in Canada.
Since the throne speech of 1974 there has been no evidence of a national medical research policy. Certainly the minister has not shown that in his philosophy medical research is the cornerstone of the health delivery and health care system. To my knowledge there is no science policy for Canada, and certainly no medical research policy. Both policies would be important, and their lack is most strange.
The minister has talked of the importance of our understanding human biology, but in the last two or three years has done little to make possible our increased understanding. I cannot recall a single instance of leadership in this field since the reading of the throne speech.
As I said earlier, any definition of human biology must involve a definition of genetics. Problems associated with genetics must be solved; and here again the minister could show leadership. In recent years we have made great strides in terms of the diagnosis of genetic illnesses and problems. Unfortunately, centres for the treatment of genetic difficulties are sporadically scattered across this coun-

try. That this should be so illustrates the rigidity of the Medical Care Act. I do not know how this rigidity will be eliminated, even with the amendments the minister has mentioned. The rigidity of the law has prevented federal and provincial cost-sharing in certain areas of medical care. I submit that genetic counselling centres should be widespread, and such counselling should be available right across the nation. Genetic counselling centres are scattered across the country. There is no national program of counselling, no national program of accreditation. In short, there is no leadership.
Many physicians do not know the great advances made in this field, developments which would help immeasurably many families. Many physicians do not know where to send people for genetic counselling. They do not know the location of the centres. I say this merely to show the minister's lack of interest in an area where the government should provide forceful federal leadership.
I do not want to talk in detail about genetic difficulties. But allow me, Madam Speaker, to make some suggestions to the minister with regard to genetic counselling. I suggest that the minister should consider calling a national conference at which experts in genetics could be brought together. I do not doubt but that such a conference would convince the minister of the importance of this particular field of medicine. There is an immediate role for the federal government in this area. I have talked about this particular health concept in the House in the past.
I have made reference to other areas to which the minister should give consideration, such as mental health, the problems of drug and alcohol abuse, cardiovascular disease, cancer, disease of the lungs, motor vehicle accidents, and problems of the aged. There are many more. However, these are some of the problems that could benefit in a very positive way by leadership from the federal government and the minister and, of course, by a rationalization of our health care system.
Time does not permit a detailed analysis of these problems, but I believe this gives some examples of the problems that could be handled by the minister and that would fit into the concept of a health care field. In my view that is being ignored by the minister. It certainly has not been fertilized by this particular bill.
As I was reading the debates I really had no intention of discussing the issue of medical manpower. I know this is of major concern to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as it is to his counterparts in the various provinces. I know there have been innumerable discussions regarding this. However, I am prompted to make a few observations having read the speech of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). I may say he made some excellent suggestions regarding the medicare bill before us. However, I was somewhat concerned about the section of his speech when he was referring to the number of doctors, specifically in the province of Quebec, and relating it to the number of doctors based on immigration. I want to quote from his speech. I quote from Hansard for January 28, 1976, page 10419:
The minister mentioned the increased number of physicians. In the last few years, the number of doctors has increased but I want to point
February 24, 1976

out to the minister that this increase was not due to the number of students coming out of university but to immigration. We have to import doctors because our students cannot enter university, since the key is in the hands of the College of Physicians. Today, there is a shortage of doctors. The minister said earlier that he was worried about a surplus of physicians, when actually there is a shortage. In the province of Quebec, we need 2,000 more doctors and yet our students are kept out of university. That is why we have to bring in immigrants, so that we may receive medical care from foreigners. I do not mind it, personally, I have nothing against them, but I would much rather see our French-Canadian students enter university freely. This is the one area in the province of Quebec where the situation is most dramatic.
I have a good deal of sympathy for the comments made by the hon. member, but I was most concerned about one sentence in his speech when he said:
We have to import doctors because our students cannot enter university, since the key is in the hands of the College of Physicians.
I wrote a short article on this point which happened to be printed in the February 20, 1976, edition of the Chatham Daily News. I think it is germane and important because there is a myth in this particular regard. I wish to quote from that article:
The Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada in presenting their brief to the Special Joint Committee of Parliament on Immigration Policy failed to address itself to the commonly held myth that the medical profession is a "closed shop" and determines the number of Canadian students admitted to medical schools.
Historically, Canada has benefited from the immigration of exceptionally talented physicians. They have played an important role in serving the public in varying capacities ranging from family physicians to leaders in the academic and research community. Interrelated with this policy of immigration is the simple economic fact that it has been less costly for government to import undergraduate students than to train them. Today foreign medical graduates now comprise about one half of all specialists certified by the College and a majority of these remain in Canada to practice their specialty.
There is, however, another side of the scenario in addition to the economic implications. First, there is the moral question of accepting a significant number of specialist physicians in particular from developing countries where their professional needs are in demand. Indeed a case can be made that Canada has developed to the point that we should be a net exporter of health services rather than an importer of health services.
The second point raised by the College is the "reverse discrimination" encouraged by our open door policy in which it is possible for foreign medical graduates to enter our system, while at the same time this privilege is denied highly qualified Canadian students who are unable to gain entrance into Canadian medical schools because of a large number of applicants with superior scholastic records.
Of course, Madam Speaker, this is the very point to which the hon. member was referring.
The brief states: "Canada should move toward training enough undergraduate medical students to meet the needs of the country as a whole. We should look forward to being able to say to Canadian citizens, 'There are enough Canadian medical students to satisfy our needs, there are enough graduate programmes to satisfy their requirements if they all stay in Canada, and there are enough jobs for all if they choose to stay here.' Some will go to the United States, Britain or Europe. We will be able to accommodate some foreign medical graduates of a calibre equal to our own. There will continue to be movement across national borders."
The long term goal for Canada has been adequately outlined in the College's summary. Canada should be self-sufficient in physician manpower, maintaining a balance and ongoing emigration of specialist physicians, and adhering to the historical tradition that this country welcomes talented new citizens.
As I was saying, Madam Speaker, I do not want to get into the area of medical manpower, but I felt for the record
Medical Care Act
it was important to destroy the myth which should have been destroyed by the college itself, but was ignored.
I want to turn for a moment to what I believe is a very basic question which has been avoided in this entire debate. The question is simply how much influence should economics have on the treatment of patients. This does not imply that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, his provincial counterparts, or indeed anyone who thinks about the problem, or any thoughtful Canadians are not concerned about receiving full value for each dollar that is spent in the health care delivery system. This does not decry the importance and the necessity of seeking alternative measures to replace high cost services with low cost services without affecting the quality of health care.
May I interject at this point and mention what I refer to as the add-on principle. I am somewhat concerned from time to time when I hear individuals in our society mention the various forms of health delivery care, noble as it may be, and say the type of service they provide may be excellent. What I am suggesting and what, I am sure, the provincial ministers are suggesting, is that if you are adding a service which is lower in cost you must be certain you are reducing something which is more costly. However, let us assume the minister is correct, that the federal government has taken a realistic stand and that health care costs should be reduced. I surely have no need to describe the effects his proposals are having on the delivery of health care in the various provinces.
Let us be realistic. The introduction of this bill and the announcement made by the former Minister of Finance in June have prompted several decisions within the province of Ontario resulting notably in the closing down of a number of hospitals and a reduction in the number of hospital beds available. The wearing of seat belts has been made mandatory. All these things are in the nature of restraints. I should not care to predict what further measures will be forced upon the provinces by such a program as we have before us, but I say to the minister in all sincerity that the unilateral action of the federal government has started a process of dilution in our health service system which will be felt in every province and every community in Canada. I have no doubt about this.
We must recognise that if we adopt this bill we are embarking on a program which must inevitably lead to mediocrity. The worst part of the legislation before us, irrespective of the amendments about which the minister spoke when he introduced the measure, is that the decisions which are made by him are all predicated on economics rather than on need. This is a factor which in my view has not received sufficient attention in the debate, yet it is a very basic question.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker. I shall try to be brief. What concerns me, as I say, is that I have the impression that the minister's attitude has really been predicated upon economics rather than needs. We are now seeing and hearing a reaction from both consumers and deliverers of the health care system; it becomes apparent that there is a feeling in the minds of the public that the quality of the health care received in the past will be prejudiced as a result of this legislation.
I might remind the minister that before the introduction of the act the very rich and the very poor always received the best of medical care. I recall that in the United States, in the City of Washington, the indigent population received the very best of care; not only did they enjoy the services of an extensive medical staff but their doctors were able to consult experts at the National Institute of Health and the Walter Reed Hospital, and so on. But how will the public react once it has experienced treatment in connection with which there has been no element of economic restraint?
How will deliverers of health care respond when they are confronted with restrictions which adversely affect the treatment of their patients? Will the public really accept diluted health systems which are predicated on economic rather than medical need? Will the public accept a system under which only the very rich may be able to afford access to the best treatment?
I believe the public will awaken and recognise that the minister is in effect proposing a second rate health care system, that the introduction of this bill, together with the announcement made by the former minister of finance in June has altogether changed the federal-provincial relationship. The minister has obviously established the priorities in his own mind and has placed concern for economics above concern for medical needs. I will only say to him that I hope he will persuade the public that public expenditure on the health care of Canadians is not a priority reduction item, particularly having regard to the funds which are spent on some other programs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend from Timiskaming was speaking a short while ago, discussing the harm which would be done to the hospitalization plan if the government proceeded with this bill. The minister interjected, saying in effect that my hon. friend was dealing with something that had no relation to the bill. He could not have been more wrong and I am sure the minister knew it. I may criticize the minister for many things but I have never thought of him as being stupid. He knew he was wrong.
The bill is one step in a calculated and well planned move on the part of the government to get out of virtually all shared cost programs. The minister said this proposal had nothing to do with hospital insurance. Madam Speaker, it limits the increase in the amount of money the federal government will pay toward a universal medical insurance plan in the next two years by specific amounts, and leaves the increase in subsequent years to be decided unilaterally by the federal government. The government has given notice to the provinces that the present agreement on hospital insurance, under the provisions of which it pays about 50 per cent of hospital insurance costs, will be ended by 1980. That date arises because the federal govern-

ment was required to give five years notice of its desire to terminate the present agreement and to enter upon a new one. The federal government is giving notice that it intends to work out a second agreement, and since it can decide for itself what it will be prepared to do in 1980, the provinces are on notice that the federal government will no longer pay the half cost it has paid up to now.
With hospitalization as with medical insurance, when Ottawa gets out of a shared cost program it has very direct consequences on the provincial governments and the people in the provinces. What can the provinces do in respect to medical or hospital insurance? If Ottawa no longer pays 50 per cent of the cost of these two programs, the provinces have a number of alternatives. For example, they can increase their own contributions to cover the deficit that will occur. All provinces, including the large have provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario, are now in financial difficulties and showing an increase in expenditure over revenue.
If the federal government cuts its percentage contribution below the increase in the cost of present or future hospital or medical insurance plans, the provinces will have to increase their contribution, and it is unlikely that they will be able to do so. In that event they will either have to cut back services or increase the revenue derived from their citizens. This can be done through deterrent fees or through a number of other methods.
We are rightly proud of our medical insurance and hospital insurance plans. When I spoke on this bill several weeks ago I talked about the federal civil servant who, when someone in the family went into a hospital in the United States, was required to put down a deposit of $1,500 before the hospital would admit that person.
Since that time I have come across the case of some friends from the city of Winnipeg who were visiting in Florida. The camper in which they were sleeping was hit by lightning during the course of an electrical storm and caught fire. The husband is now in hospital; he has been there for three weeks and will probably be there for another three weeks. The cost of the hospital alone, not including any medical bills, in Florida is over $2,000 a week. I would suggest there are very few people in this country or in any other country who could afford to meet this kind of bill.
If people do not have to worry about completely wiping out their life's savings at the present time to pay hospital bills, it is because we have a universal hospital insurance plan in this country. This kind of universal plan has taken away the fear of financial disaster from Canadian citizens, but the plan will disappear as the federal government's limitation on the amount of money it pays for hospital and medical insurance plans begins to bite.
A similar process has now begun in the field of postsecondary education. Having persuaded the provinces to expand vastly their university and community college programs begun in 1972, the federal government has put a ceiling of 15 per cent on the increased amount it will pay each year. Post-secondary education costs have been rising by a very substantial amount each year. In a recent study that was made of the Canadian educational system by an
February 24, 1976

OECD committee, Canada was given high marks for the tremendous job done by the federal and provincial governments in improving the educational system of this country. The study showed the tremendous increase in the number of students attending elementary and secondary schools as well as the large number of people attending post-secondary institutions, such as our universities, community colleges, and manpower training programs.
All the provinces have done an excellent job in this regard, to a large extent as a result of the financial inducements offered to them by the federal government. At a time when costs began increasing very rapidly, the federal government a couple of years ago put a ceiling on the increase that it would pay in any year of 15 per cent. The present agreement with the provinces expires in March, 1977, and there has been no indication given by the federal government that it is prepared to renew the agreement with the provinces, to improve it, or to do anything else. Indeed no discussions at all have been held with the provinces. It is not at all unlikely, given the example of medical and hospital insurance which we are now discussing, that in 1977 the federal government will cut the 15 per cent ceiling which it has already introduced unilaterally.
A similar situation existed in the welfare field. It was not many years ago that a Liberal government introduced the Canada Assistance Plan. We were given the most glowing description of what a great plan it was, how it was the culmination of a quarter century or more of Liberal party thought, planning, studies, and promises of a comprehensive social security system.
This plan has been in effect for only a few years, and lo and behold the minister has now given notice that he intends to introduce a social services act to come into effect in 1977. This is an act that will run parallel with the present Canada Assistance Plan for three years, after which time the Canada Assistance Plan will disappear.
It seems that the minister and his government have had second thoughts about universal fees, users' charges, and deterrent fees. We are talking about programs which are not even completely in place yet. We are also talking about expansion of day-care centres. I saw a report in today's newspaper about the minister meeting with a group of women and promising an expansion of day-care centres. We are also talking about nursing homes of which there are certainly not enough. If there is any hope that we can cut back on the sharp and continually increasing cost of hospitalization, surely one of the ways to do so is to establish adequate nursing homes and convalescent hospitals which would be much cheaper than the high cost, intensive hospitalization plans which the federal government now funds.
These are plans that are not yet funded, or funded on any regular, continuing basis, but which the provinces understand. Yet already the minister has given an indication that the federal government intends to cut back on the agreements it has with the provinces under the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan.
In the field of manpower there have been unilateral and continuing cutbacks in grants for training programs in all provinces. What has happened? The provinces got into the
Medical Care Act
delivery of manpower training largely because of what I believe was the mistaken concept of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government that the federal government has no business in the field of education, and that this is solely the responsibility of the provinces.
It was felt that the federal government could and should be involved in manpower training. However, Ottawa did not establish its own manpower centres. It contracted with the provinces and with local educational divisions to use their facilities. Facilities were built and extended, teachers were hired, and equipment was purchased, to a large extent to provide for the manpower training needs as defined by the federal department of manpower. Because of the financial constraints the federal government has unilaterally begun to cut back on manpower training agreements with the provinces. It- has cut back on the purchase of manpower training equipment in the community colleges and other institutions in the provinces.
Let us consider the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. At a time when the have-not provinces, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, northern Ontario and northern Saskatchewan were experiencing sharp increases in unemployment-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: And eastern Quebec.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Yes, and eastern Quebec, and I wish the hon. member who made that interjection would get up and support me in the case I am making. At a time when these areas are experiencing sharp increases in unemployment and in welfare costs, DREE is at best holding the line. There are virtually no increases in the funds of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Holding the line in a period when we have had a 10 per cent or more increase in inflation in each of the last two or three years means a cutback in the real money that can be spent to provide jobs in these areas.
Let us look at the department which supposedly was established to protect the rights and meet the needs of the most deprived people in this country, and I am talking about the native people, the Indians and Eskimos. At a time when costs are skyrocketing the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been chipping away at the expenditures it is prepared to make to provide for the health and welfare needs of our native people.
For example, when the province of Saskatchewan inaugurated a program of providing hearing aids for people who need them Ottawa said it was not going to pay for hearing aids for native people in Saskatchewan. How cheap can the government get? These are the programs the federal government decided to implement unilaterally.
I put these facts on the record not because I believe everything the provinces do is right, and not only because I am concerned about the very rapid and substantial increase in the cost of medical plans. Of course I am concerned about that. I am concerned about that as a member of parliament, as a citizen who has to pay the increases himself and whose constituents have to pay the increases.
The point surely is that when Ottawa gets out of these programs or limits its contributions to them, the shortfall

February 24, 1976
Medical Care Act
of funds must be picked up by the provinces or by the individual citizen, regardless, and I emphasize that word "regardless", of their ability or inability to pay. This is why I am concerned.
We have had a health insurance plan and a hospital insurance plan in this country for many years; in the case of the health insurance plan, for more than ten years, and in the case of the hospital insurance plan for more than 20 years. During that time the federal government has not administered any of these programs, not the hospitalization or the medical insurance plans. They have been organized, run and operated by the provinces. The provinces have the experience. Ottawa does not have that experience or the know-how.
I would say the provinces of Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec must be more concerned about the rapid increase in the cost of medical insurance and the implications to their financial structures than is the federal government, because they are much less able to raise the money through taxation, deterrent fees or in any other way than is the federal government. They are concerned, but they are and have been willing from the beginning to meet at the official or at the ministerial level to work out in detail plans which can be made at least to begin to halt the constant escalation in costs.
Despite many promises by the minister, going back to 1973 at least, that the federal government would not implement changes unilaterally, that has not been the case. The minister and the government have broken all their promises to the provinces. Not many months ago the minister promised the provinces that his deputy would meet with provincial deputy ministers on March 16 and 17 to discuss cost-sharing programs and reforms that could be made to save money.
The minister agreed to meet with provincial ministers of health on April 27 and 28. That will be the first meeting since January 1975, to discuss this question. The minister has been meeting with individual provincial ministers of health. He has refused for more than a year to meet with them jointly. I can only assume that he thought by meeting with them individually he could drive a wedge between them.
I presume it is evidence of the minister's good faith that he is going to meet with provincial ministers of health to discuss in a friendly way methods of slowing down increasing costs of medical care without the necessity of using the big stick or threat of this bill. If the minister is interested in discussions and agreements rather than in confrontation and unilateral decisions he ought to agree to the amendment proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), which would set this bill aside at least until after the minister has met with provincial ministers to see whether an agreement can be reached.
If the minister insists on continuing with this bill then we can only assume that he and the government have no intention or desire to reach an agreement with the provinces which would be mutually acceptable to all the provinces and the federal government. We would have to assume that the minister intends to implement this despite

the feelings of the provinces; that is, that he intends to make unilateral decisions in respect of cutting back on the shared cost program about which I have spoken.
We are talking about an extremely serious matter. We are talking about programs which cost the provinces not hundreds of dollars but more than $1,000 million for health insurance alone, the cost of which Ottawa does not now share with the provinces. It is no wonder the provinces are worried, are frightened, and are apprehensive. Given the kind of stubbornness and arrogance the minister has shown, the provinces, to say the least, are frightened sick.
I should like to spend a little time placing on the record the feelings of the provinces. Let me emphasize again that while I may be speaking in the main of the position of the government of Manitoba on this question, all the provinces are united in their objection to this bill and to the proposals being made by the minister. If we look over the list of the provinces we will see that the Conservative government of Newfoundland, the Liberal government of Nova Scotia, the Conservative government of New Brunswick, the Liberal government of Quebec-with which I think the minister has a good deal of relationship-the Conservative government of Ontario, the NDP governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, the Conservative government of Alberta, and although I have not seen anything specific I believe, the Social Credit government of British Columbia, as was the former NDP government of British Columbia, are united in their opposition.
The provinces have agreed to undertake a broad analysis in an attempt to define more precisely those concerns they have voiced in discussions over the past couple of years with the minister and his government. They have carried on some studies which show that most provinces would experience a serious shortfall in revenues under the proposal for a GNP escalator plan, even with the so-called risk sharing modifications the minister proposed.
Their studies showed that the proposed thrust funds would be barely adequate to cover these shortfalls in some provinces and would be far from sufficient to offset losses experienced in other provinces. The studies showed that most provinces have committed themselves in recent years to improving their services to bring about greater efficiencies despite the fact that these efforts are not supported by any cost-sharing assistance from the federal government. Their commitment in total terms is such that they cannot afford to consider, much less accept, any financing formula which would provide even less assistance to the provinces than they have been receiving up until now.
According to their joint study the ten provinces were spending last year a total of over $1.2 billion a year in respect of health programs for which there is no cost sharing available. They have calculated that by the fiscal year 1978-79 their expenditures will increase to $1.9 billion annually. What is happening is that when the provinces devise programs which are much less expensive than programs now jointly funded, they cannot obtain any money from the federal government even if they can demonstrate that the cost of such programs is substantially less than the present programs.
Let me give two illustrations. The province of Saskatchewan has inaugurated a nurse-practitioner program. Through this program a registered nurse is given further
February 24, 1976

training so that she can deal with many of the health needs of the people who live in rural areas, in small areas or villages where there is not now medical service available. It should be obvious to the minister and to the government first of all that this is a needed service which has not been met in recent years in Saskatchewan, and I am sure in similar areas in other provinces where there is a shortage of doctors. Instead of encouraging such a program, and encouraging its expansion into other areas of Saskatchewan and other areas in other provinces, this program is not jointly funded by the federal government.
Several years ago the province of Manitoba inaugurated a program which is partially funded by the federal government. It is called "New Careers". Under this program the provincial government hires and trains native people and immigrants to work for the province in areas not now provided with health or welfare services.
These people, who very often do not even have a high school education, are given training for a period of from six weeks to a year to perform specific jobs in the field of health such as giving inoculations and performing other services which up until now have been carried out by doctors or registered nurses. These people work in areas where there are not sufficient doctors or registered nurses.
This program has been a tremendous success. It has been lauded by a number of federal government departments. This program cannot expand because it is not cost-shared by the federal government unless the federal government looks at every job and every training program that is inaugurated. Such programs should be encouraged because in this way services are provided more cheaply than are the nursing services now provided under the present system.
What is happening? Just when the provinces are developing programs, the federal government has decided unilaterally to cut back on the money which it pays them. As I have said on other occasions, and as I have said earlier tonight, I am not opposed to consideration by all levels of government of ways and means of cutting back on increased expenditure, but the way not to do it is by the kind of unilateral decision which is made by the government and proposed in this bill.
As I have said, the provinces have looked at what they are paying out in order to meet the health needs of their people. The estimates which they have made suggest that the total health care expenditure in the ten provinces, including federal shared cost support, will probably rise between 15 per cent and 20 per cent in the next year, an increase of more than $1 billion over the estimated $6.6 billion which was spent by the provincial governments in the last fiscal year. Given that tremendous problem, the provincial health ministers arrived at a number of conclusions among which I want to refer to just two.
In January of 1975 they agreed at a meeting which they held in Ottawa, first, that each province should receive no less federal financial support than it would have received for the funding of health insurance programs under the current arrangement; second, that new financing arrangements must allow the provinces flexibility to pursue programs in accordance with their own particular priorities;
Medical Care Act
third, that the new arrangements must allow for equitable cost sharing of both the start-up and continuing operating costs of new programs, as well as changes within existing programs; and fourth, that new arrangements should relate to health goals and objectives, and should provide encouragement to new provincial programs which offer alternatives to high cost services. Examples of such alternatives include home care, geriatric services, community health services, and ambulatory care.
That kind of proposal has not even been discussed with the federal minister, not because the provinces have not been willing but because the minister has simply refused to meet with them. Yet on the day that that meeting was held in Ottawa, the minister held a press conference. I want to put on the record a couple of paragraphs from the interview which he gave for the press and which was reported in the Ottawa Journal of January 15, 1975. They read:
The federal government may soon be contributing more money toward the cost of the country's health services . ..
He told reporters at the federal-provincial health ministers conference that a committee will be set up to study cost-sharing legislation to see if the federal government can, under present laws, help pay for alternative provincial health services.
That committee has not yet met, and the minister has not yet met with the provinces. It is not surprising therefore that the provinces, to say the least, were highly critical and very vocal in their criticism of the minister and of his proposal.
On August 19, 1975, the provincial health ministers met in Victoria. Let me quote what some of them said, as reported in the Victoria Colonist of August 19, 1975, as follows:
Health ministers from all ten Canadian provinces were unanimous Monday in their criticism of proposed new federal health service costsharing formulas ...
Saskatchewan Health Minister Walter Smishek charged that the federal government had misled the provinces over cost-sharing formulas for health services. He said the federal government had bargained "in bad faith, misled the provinces, and as a result left them to pick up large, increasing bills which were to have been shared by Ottawa".
In case the minister would suggest that this is a criticism which is politically partisan coming as it did from an NDP health minister, let me quote what the Liberal health minister from the province of Nova Scotia, Mr. MacEachen, said. He was concerned that the tapering off of federal financing can seriouly affect health care in his province, and he said:
"If the federal government is suggesting that it has solved the problems of inflation, then the limitations proposed on increases of medical care payments may not have too great an effect... if, however, general inflation carries on at or near its present rate, we could be in serious difficulty.
When the premiers met in August of 1975 in Newfoundland, they passed a resolution which is as follows. I will just give the last part of it because my time is limited. It reads:
Be it therefore resolved that the Prime Minister of Canada be requested to convene a conference of first ministers to consider the present shared cost programs and the future of such programs with particular reference to the fields of hospital insurance and medicare, currently the subject of concern, and to consider ways in which the Government of Canada and the provinces, together, can control the

February 24, 1976
Adjournment Debate
costs of shared cost programs in the most effective manner, consistent with desirable standards of service.
That was an excellent, well documented, well thought out resolution. I suggest to the minister that he could give meaning to that resolution by agreeing to the proposal made by my colleague the hon. member for Broadview, that this bill be stood over for six months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the one or two minutes available to me I will make just a few remarks and then perhaps continue at the next sitting.
I had no intention of rising to speak on this bill. However, it does perturb me to hear hon. members from opposition parties stand in the House and speak against many aspects of Bill C-68 and indeed against the content of the bill because, after all, what the government is attempting to do with this bill is, I suggest, a very important thing, namely, it is endeavouring to show leadership in the area of restraint, a matter that is extremely important in the eyes of so many Canadians today when ordinary people at all levels and in all walks of life are being asked to show restraint in terms of wages, and industries, big and large, are being asked to show restraint in terms of prices.
I think the government needs to be commended rather than criticized for endeavouring to take action which shows restraint in an area of great expenditure.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: CITIZENSHIP-REQUEST THAT VACANCIES IN TORONTO CITIZENSHIP COURTS BE FILLED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
CITIZENSHIP-REQUEST THAT VACANCIES IN TORONTO CITIZENSHIP COURTS BE FILLED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the abundant natural resources of Canada provided the material foundation for our country, and immigration provided the human resources to build and develop this great land which is the envy of the world. Since the dawn of Canadian history, successive waves of immigrants have come to our land from every continent on this planet. Canada's population has in fact increased faster than that of any other industrialized country in the twentieth century.
I should like also to state that it was to a great extent the freedoms we enjoy in Canada as well as the economic prosperity, and lately the federal government's enlightened policy of multiculturalism, which has attracted so many immigrants to this land and also encouraged them to become full citizens. In fact the total intake of immigrants to Canada since 1945 is nearly 4 million. This new wave of immigration brought to us people with great experience of life, rich human values, and plenty of special skills which
(Mr. Orlikow.]
contributed immensely to our economic growth and prosperity.
It should also be noted that the net immigration since the end of the second world war is approximately 3 million or slightly less. However, from 1947 to 1971 only 1,529,853 Canadian citizenship certificates were granted by our courts.
Once upon a time, at least until 1967, we had in Canada a department of citizenship and immigration, and since 1967 citizenship comes under the Department of the Secretary of State. But it was only since 1970 that a great impetus was given to citizenship matters. In that year a revitalized program of citizenship was launched. It was based on a five point policy, namely, certain objectives such as the reinforcement of Canadian identity and national unity, the encouragement of cultural diversification within the bilingual framework, the preservation of human rights and fundamental freedoms, an increased and vastly improved citizenship participation program, and the development of meaningful symbols of Canadian sovereignty. As a result, in 1974 alone, 130,278 persons were granted Canadian citizenship certificates in our courts.
Later an outreach program to increase the number of people applying for citizenship and to make that process much easier was launched by our government. As a result, storefront citizenship offices and additional courts such as those in Parkdale's Dufferin Plaza, Kensington in the Spadina constituency, and at Montreal's Jean Talon Street added greatly to the number of applications.
Today the 21 citizenship judges have a very heavy overload to clear up, especially in the city of Toronto. More applicants will increase the workload for these courts with the advent of the new Citizenship Act, which was debated at second reading in this House and is now being studied by a House of Commons committee. This new enlightened legislation is not only liberal and progressive, but also very attractive to the people who are waiting to become Canadian citizens. I must say that this legislation is most welcome. The government and the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) are to be commended for bringing this piece of legislation to this House.
However, more funds for more qualified judges and support staff are needed without further delay. As I stated in my question to the Secretary of State last February 10, we are impatiently awaiting the appointment of more judges and staff in Toronto and other places where they are needed. The backlog must be cleared up quickly because qualified applicants are waiting to become Canadian citizens and to take their full place in the Canadian sun.
Any further undue delay would be denying the privileges of Canadian citizenship to many people. As the dictum goes, justice delayed is justice denied, and the sooner the necessary staff is provided for our citizenship courts, the better will be the morale of the present staff and also the earlier will Canada be strengthened with many more loyal citizens.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CITIZENSHIP-REQUEST THAT VACANCIES IN TORONTO CITIZENSHIP COURTS BE FILLED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Faulkner) has been assured by the Registrar of Citizenship that the citizenship applications and certifi-
February 24, 1976

cate presentations in the Toronto area have been carefully looked into as a result of the hon. member's question. He has further been informed that the backlog alluded to is not as serious as suggested.
As an example and with reference to the St. Clair citizenship court, there were only 581 certificates on hand as of February 12, all of which will have been presented by February 26. For the information of this House it should be known that this particular citizenship court now has a scheduling whereby certificates are presented within 14 days of receipt from Ottawa. The 14 days in question are used for scheduling the ceremonies and informing the applicants.
With reference to the Dufferin court it had, as of February 12, some 726 certificates on hand, 400 of which will be distributed this month. Although another 300 certificates will have been received for presentation before the end of the month, this is not an unduly large number of certificates to have on hand in courts as large as the two to which I have referred.
In 1975, through our Toronto courts' system only, a total of over 49,000 grants of citizenship were made. This figure includes those grants made through storefront offices, the mobile team, and the subcourts in Oshawa, Brampton and Barrie. In addition to the large number of grants of citizenship processed by the Toronto citizenship court system, there were 36,391 proofs of citizenship given out in 1975. These proofs do not, of course, involve a court ceremony and presentation but nevertheless account for a large volume of work by court personnel.
I would also like to take the opportunity to say a word about the success of the citizenship outreach program, since I believe it has a bearing on the questions raised by the hon. member. The storefront concept was introduced in Toronto in July 1973, which means there have been two and a half years of storefront operation.
In 1975 there were 13,420 storefront grant applications, an increase of 21 per cent over the previous year. There were almost 4,000 proof applications processed in the storefront offices, a percentage increase of 53 per cent. There would seem, however, to be no need at the present time to increase staff in the Toronto court system beyond the filling of existing vacancies.
The effect of the outreach program has been to relieve the overburdened situation at the St. Clair office which, until 1973, was the only citizenship registration office in Toronto. With the opening of the Dufferin court in July, 1975, and with the outreach services provided by storefront and mobile operations, grants volume in the St. Clair court decreased by 10 per cent in 1975.
With respect to citizenship hearings, no backlog exists vis-a-vis the St. Clair court. There is, however, a one-month delay at the Dufferin court which involves approximately 600 applications. A delay in hearings also exists at Barrie and Brampton involving approximately 250 applicants. This situation will be corrected when a new citizenship judge is appointed.
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF FRENCH LANGUAGE COVERAGE OF CONSERVATIVE CONVENTION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF FRENCH LANGUAGE COVERAGE OF CONSERVATIVE CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked if the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) had been made aware of complaints concerning the inadequate French language television coverage of the Progressive Conservative convention and if it was the intention of the minister to remind the publicly financed Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of its primary responsibility to report in both official languages all public affairs of national interest. The minister replied that the corporation had a responsibility to report important events in both official languages on both channels.
Last Thursday the hon. member for Cumberland-Col-chester North (Mr. Coates) expressed his dissatisfaction with programmed CBC radio coverage in his area.
Earlier today the hon. member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) proposed, by way of a motion under Standing Order 43, to refer the subject to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts. The motion required unanimous consent which, unfortunately, was not forthcoming. I say unfortunately, because it is my opinion that a dissenting voice came from among the members of the party that was considerably disenchanted with the treatment accorded that party by the publicly owned television network.
During the question period today a member of the official opposition, I believe the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), again raised the subject of inadequate French language television coverage of the Progressive Conservative convention. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Miss Campbell) replied, giving information supplied by the CBC and which, in my opinion, was no answer at all. It was a reiteration of what programming there was and did not answer the question.
We are already aware of the amount of coverage accorded by the French network of the CBC. As Joan Irwin stated so well in an article in yesterday's Montreal Gazette, and I quote:
Both English networks made a major commitment to the Canadian public by providing an opportunity to participate in an important political event. They deserve our gratitude.
French-speaking Canadians, on the other hand, had almost no opportunity to acquaint themselves with the PC leadership candidates or with the political philosophies of a major national party at a crucial moment in its history.
It's not particularly surprising that TeleMetropole and the TVA network ignored the whole thing until the results of the voting were known.
It is surprising and entirely indefensible that the CBC French network showed so little interest in the convention or in the rights of its audience to be well informed on vital national issues.
Radio-Canada carried none of Saturday's convention live during the speeches of the 12 leadership candidates, despite the fact that three candidates were from Quebec-and two of them front-runners for the leadership.
Not until 11:10 p.m. (after the hockey game and the news) did Radio-Canada give its audience a glimpse of the convention, and then only in edited bits of each candidate's speech-of which many were poorly translated by an extremely uncertain male translator.

February 24, 1976
Adjournment Debate
On Sunday, Radio-Canada had intended to devote only the six to eight p.m. period to the convention. Then it said it would begin its coverage at four p.m.
Finally someone in the French network saw the light, and it was announced that Sunday's coverage would begin at 2:30 p.m.
The indecision and irresponsibility of the French network indicate an alarming narrowness of view and curious perception of the tax-supported corporation's obligations to the Canadian public-all the Canadian public.
The estimates have now been tabled. Included in those of the Secretary of State is the sum of $416 million for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, an increase over last year for operating expenditures alone of over $50 million.
Whenever I question the present Secretary of State, and also when I questioned his predecessor, I was lectured on independence and the inability of the Secretary of State to interfere. They argue that they have no legal right to meddle in the affairs on an independent corporation. Well, I have news for the Secretary of State. As long as taxpayers in my constituency see vast sums of their tax moneys being poured into a corporation which services only an average 11 per cent of the population, they are going to be on my back, and rightly so. In turn, I am going to expect the Secretary of State to come up with answers.
I am sure the minister will not forget the political indiscretion that I committed in 1973 by proposing in committee a nominal cut in the estimates to indicate that the politician still had some say in the publicly financed CBC. That motion passed with the help of some of my more experienced colleagues. Whilst I may not take such a step again, I do want to point out that there must be some established line of communication between those who spend the money and those who are responsible for paying the bills.
The Progressive Conservative party may not be strong in its parliamentary representation from Quebec, but its total
percentage vote in that province is healthy. However, apart from that party's supporters, there were those from all other parties and those with no political affiliation who wanted to watch the convention proceedings.
The English coverage extended over four days. It was generally well handled. Why were French Canadians shafted by the television channel which owes its very existence to the considerable financial support of the taxpayer; as I said earlier, $416 million?
May I request that an inquiry be instituted and a full statement made to all members of this House on this continuing saga of complete irresponsibility.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF FRENCH LANGUAGE COVERAGE OF CONSERVATIVE CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has been informed by the CBC that the CBC French television network covered the final day of the convention, Sunday, February 24, from 2:30 p.m. to the end of the convention at 9:10 p.m.
On the Saturday of the convention, a resume of the speeches of the candidates was telecast from 11:10 p.m. until 12:40 a.m. A live telecast of the candidates' speeches would have involved five hours of almost continuous simultaneous translation which could have been a great strain for the television audience. The exigencies of production, i.e., the condensing in as polished a fashion as possible of the five hours from the afternoon, required a late evening scheduling of the resume.
The "Stanfield Evening" on the Friday of the convention was telecast in its entirety, and an hour of the Diefenbaker tribute was telecast on Thursday.
A total of 11 hours of the convention were scheduled on the CBC French television network as compared with eight and one half hours at the last Progressive Conservative convention in 1967.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.17 p.m.

Wednesday, February 25, 1976
